matched.set_a_axis: From self-sovereign heroic agency to repentant interdependence
matched.set_b_axis: From sovereign self-assertion to humble interdependence
matched.overlap_description: Both trace a movement from self-crowning chivalric agency and instrumental use of others toward dependence, repentance, and communal reconciliation.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-sealing enchantment logic to lucid disenchantment
matched.set_b_axis: From enchantment-sustained certainty to lucid self-renunciation
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Don Quixote's romance-saturated certitude, his enchantment-based rationalizations, and his final recovery of reason and rejection of knight-errantry.

matched.set_a_axis: From invented knight-errant to reconciled mortal self
matched.set_b_axis: From honor-seeking renown to repentant Christian humility
matched.overlap_description: These are a loose match: A emphasizes the invented chivalric identity and title accumulation, while B emphasizes honor, fame, and public renown. Both end in the rejection of the chivalric self in favor of a humble Christian mortal identity.

unique_to_a.axis: From honor-driven blame-shifting to merciful self-accountability

unique_to_b.axis: From euphoric-volatile self-righteousness to calm resignation

matched.set_a_axis: From instrumental command to affectionate reciprocal partnership
matched.set_b_axis: From instrumental patronage to grateful, affectionate partnership
matched.overlap_description: Both describe the Sancho relationship as moving from patronizing recruitment and instrumental command toward trust, esteem, emotional dependence, apology, and final blessing.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-authored ideal to anxious rescue fantasy and final relinquishment
matched.set_b_axis: From absolutized lady-fantasy to discarded chivalric illusion
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Dulcinea as a self-authored literary ideal that becomes an enchantment-rescue obsession and is finally abandoned when Don Quixote renounces the chivalric frame.

unique_to_a.axis: From impatient evasion to familial reconciliation

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From sovereign heroic self-assertion to humble interdependence
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A self-asserting, dominance-oriented fantasist who renames himself, invents Dulcinea, recruits Sancho through promises, imposes chivalric categories on reality, and treats other people chiefly as audience, instruments, or obstacles to his solitary heroic mission.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: A defeated, sane man who relinquishes heroic self-assertion, confesses his madness, apologizes to Sancho, rewards household servants, submits to God and the sacraments, and dies as Alonso Quixano among family, friends, and dependents, recognizing dependence and moral debt.

trajectory.position_description: Strongly agency-driven: he manufactures a knightly identity, names horse, self, and lady, reads the inn as a castle, demands dubbing, and enlists Sancho as an instrument and audience for his romance script.
key_moments: Loses his wits reading chivalry books and decides to become a knight-errant.
Names himself Don Quixote, his horse Rocinante, and invents Dulcinea as Lady of Thoughts.
Demands to be dubbed a knight and attacks carriers who disturb his armor.
Recruits Sancho with promises of an island governorship.

trajectory.position_description: Agency remains dominant but becomes hierarchical and coercive: he commands Sancho, punishes mockery, and explains every contradiction as enchantment. Dependence on Sancho grows, but communion remains patronizing rather than reciprocal.
key_moments: Charges windmills and converts failure into the Sage Freston's malice.
Frees galley slaves and demands their embassy to Dulcinea.
Performs the Sierra Morena penance and sends Sancho to Dulcinea.
Beats or threatens Sancho over Dulcinea and the lashes.
Is caged and carted home while interpreting captivity as enchantment.

trajectory.phase: Inflated public agency and staged performance
trajectory.position_description: His agency becomes theatrical and literary: he seeks fame, printed history, staged combats, and courtly recognition. He remains commanding, but increasingly depends on Sancho, hosts, and enchanters to sustain his role.
key_moments: Undertakes the third sally and defends chivalric truth.
Experiences El Toboso disillusion and the peasant-girl enchantment.
Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and confronts the lion.
Participates in Clavileño and the staged duenna adventures.

trajectory.position_description: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon strips him of active mastery. He accepts retirement, delegates judgment to Sancho, stops Sancho's whipping out of compassion, and returns home subdued and dependent.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and must retire for a year.
Endures pig stampede, mock resurrection, and ducal humiliations.
Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out in pain.
Admits his wits are confused and lets Sancho judge the peasants' dispute.

trajectory.position_description: He surrenders agency to Christian humility and communal obligation. He renounces knight-errantry, asks forgiveness, makes bequests, blesses Sancho, and dies lucid among others.
key_moments: Wakes sane and renounces books of chivalry as dark ignorance.
Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into mad knight-errantry and cancels his debts.
Calls his niece and housekeeper his daughters and provides for them in his will.
Dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The arc begins with a solitary hidalgo imposing a self-authored heroic identity on the world and commanding others as romance figures; it ends with a defeated, sane man acknowledging dependence on Sancho and his household, seeking forgiveness, and dying within ordinary Christian community.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-sealing enchantment logic to lucid disenchantment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Absolute conviction that chivalric romances are literal truth and that he is a knight-errant; inns are castles, windmills are giants, strangers are knights or enchanters, and every contradiction is the work of hostile enchanters rather than his own error.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Full lucidity: he admits his madness, calls chivalry books detestable absurdities, rejects the pastoral fantasy, renounces Don Quixote, confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies sane as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Reality is wholly assimilated to romance. His identity is unquestioned, and defeats are rationalized rather than doubted.
key_moments: Dubbing at the inn and armor-watching.
Mistakes windmills for giants and blames the sage Freston.
Frees galley slaves and interprets their ingratitude as villainy.
Treats the basin as Mambrino's helmet and rationalizes its appearance.

trajectory.position_description: He can say that he pictures Dulcinea as he wishes and chooses Amadis-style penance deliberately, yet this insight is absorbed into the chivalric frame. Contradictions become proof of hostile enchantment.
key_moments: Admits poets invent ladies and that he imagines Dulcinea.
Chooses Amadis-style penance as a deliberate performance.
Describes the cave of Montesinos vision and insists on its truth.
Sees a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea and blames enchanters.

trajectory.position_description: Staged courtly adventures validate him outwardly, but the false Second Part, the Knight of the Mirrors, and doubts about the cave vision increasingly destabilize his confidence.
key_moments: Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and explains Samson's face as an enchanter's transformation.
Hears the enchanted head and staged Merlin confirm Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Begins to doubt whether his cave vision was true.
Accepts Clavileño and Merlin literally despite earlier doubts.

trajectory.position_description: After the White Moon defeat he becomes more rational about ordinary matters such as inns and false histories, but still believes in enchantment, Sancho's penance, and omens. Delusion persists alongside genuine self-reproach.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and accepts a year's retirement.
Recognizes an inn as an inn and admits his wits are confused.
Reads the hare as an omen despite earlier condemning superstition.
Still hopes for Dulcinea's disenchantment.

trajectory.position_description: The delusion breaks completely. He recognizes his madness, repents, renounces knight-errantry, and frames his former heroism as dangerous illusion.
key_moments: Wakes from fever with his reason clear and calls chivalry books detestable absurdities.
Rejects the pastoral plan as nonsense and insists he is no longer Don Quixote.
Confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The novel tracks a long, non-linear consolidation of delusional certitude through repeated enchantment rationalizations, followed by late doubts under staged and real mirrors, then a final deathbed recovery of reason.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From chivalric self-myth and fame to humble mortal salvation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A modest hidalgo refashions himself as Don Quixote de la Mancha, accumulates chivalric titles, treats identity as a literary script to be proved by fame, and pursues eternal renown, honor, imperial rank, and public recognition through deeds dedicated to Dulcinea and posterity.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He rejects the Don Quixote identity as madness, insists he is Alonso Quixano, renounces chivalric glory, seeks confession, charity, fidelity, and forgiveness above fame, makes a sane Christian will, and dies as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Identity is invented through names and props: Don Quixote, Rocinante, Dulcinea, and the mock dubbing all confirm a new self. Renown is already the explicit goal.
key_moments: Takes the name Don Quixote de La Mancha after naming his horse and lady.
Believes the innkeeper's mock ceremony makes him a genuine knight.
Desires to become Emperor of Trebizond and win eternal name.
Demands the Toledo traders confess Dulcinea's beauty.

trajectory.position_description: Identity becomes increasingly public and literary: he adopts titles, treats printed history as proof of his reality, and makes honor legalistic and theatrical.
key_moments: Adopts the nickname Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
Renames himself Knight of the Lions after confronting the lion.
Defends fictional Queen Madasima with his life.
Rejoices that a printed history of his deeds exists and worries about reputation.

trajectory.position_description: His authentic identity is challenged by public performance, the false Second Part, and then shattered by the White Moon defeat. He begins to imagine a diminished pastoral alias, Quixotize.
key_moments: Seeks public vindication at Saragossa, in Barcelona, and before the duke and duchess.
Reads the false Second Part and resolves to disprove it by going to Barcelona.
Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and calls himself the most unfortunate knight.
Plans a pastoral retirement with the alias Quixotize.

trajectory.position_description: He rejects the pastoral alias and the entire knightly self. His final identity is the sane, penitent Alonso Quixano, and salvation replaces renown.
key_moments: Calls the pastoral plan nonsense and says he is no longer Don Quixote.
Insists he is Alonso Quixano, enemy of Amadis and all knight-errantry.
Makes a will and provides for his household.
Dies as Alonso Quixano the Good, with the curate testifying to his sanity.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The identity and honor arc moves from self-naming and title accumulation through public fame and counterfeit doubles to a final deathbed rejection of the invented knight in favor of the ordinary mortal name and Christian humility.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From honor-driven blame-shifting to merciful self-accountability
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Moral reasoning is mimetic chivalric honor: violence proves virtue, suffering confers honor, failures are enchanters' fault, and Sancho's body is instrumental to Dulcinea's cure.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He recognizes harm done to Sancho, stops the whipping when Sancho cries out, apologizes for drawing him into madness, cancels debts, seeks forgiveness, and makes amends in his will.

trajectory.position_description: He acts from romance scripts, rescues Andres, frees galley slaves, and attacks supposed villains, while rationalizing harmful outcomes as ingratitude or enchantment.
key_moments: Forces Juan Haldudo to promise payment to Andres, then leaves him vulnerable.
Frees the galley slaves and is beaten by them.
Blames Sancho for warning him about the galley slaves and for contradicting his fantasies.

trajectory.position_description: His devotion to Dulcinea and his honor justifies coercing Sancho and dismissing Sancho's judgment, though protectiveness and gratitude occasionally break through.
key_moments: Threatens to tie Sancho and whip him to disenchant Dulcinea.
Beats Sancho for disparaging Dulcinea.
Rescues Sancho during the boar hunt and defends him from the servants' prank.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat, he becomes more capable of restraint and dependence: he delegates judgment to Sancho and stops the penance when Sancho is in pain.
key_moments: Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out and covers him with his cloak.
Admits he is unfit to judge and lets Sancho settle the peasants' wager.
Praises Sancho as a great philosopher and accepts his counsel.

trajectory.position_description: He accepts responsibility for Sancho and his household, renounces the harmful books, apologizes, and seeks Christian forgiveness.
key_moments: Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into knight-errantry.
Cancels Sancho's debts and promises him rewards in his will.
Protects his niece from chivalry books and asks forgiveness of the false author.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Moral reasoning evolves from honor-driven violence and external blame toward mercy, restraint, and explicit accountability, culminating in the apology to Sancho and the penitent will.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From euphoric-volatile self-righteousness to calm resignation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He is emotionally volatile: euphoric in fantasy, anxious about chivalric procedure, furious when contradicted, physically violent toward Sancho and strangers, and prone to self-dramatizing despair or exaltation.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: In his final state he is calm, devout, tender, self-accusing, and resigned to death. The rage and theatrical self-pity are gone, replaced by sober repentance and affection.

trajectory.position_description: Mood swings rapidly from joy to anxiety to rage to self-pity. Violence and rhetoric are immediate responses to contradiction.
key_moments: Euphoria at being dubbed.
Rage at traders and carriers.
Beats Sancho over Dulcinea.
Fulling-mill humiliation and rage.

trajectory.phase: Righteous volatility under a chivalric code
trajectory.position_description: Anger is often legalistic and self-justifying, but he can also be serene and didactic. Mood remains reactive to honor, Dulcinea, and enchantment.
key_moments: Attacks Cardenio over a fictional queen.
Threatens violence during Micomicona adventures.
Delivers the serene Golden Age speech.
Remains stoic while caged.

trajectory.position_description: He oscillates between exultant performance and humiliation: lions, Clavileño, mock resurrection, and courtly mockery provoke grandiosity, alarm, and self-justification.
key_moments: Lion episode and renaming as Knight of the Lions.
Dulcinea enchantment despair.
Castle humiliations.
Mock resurrection and pressure on Sancho.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat his volatility cools into melancholy, self-reproach, and resignation. He still has flashes of irritation, but the dominant tone is weary acceptance.
key_moments: Broods over defeat.
Calls his wits confused.
Endures pig stampede and abduction.
Returns home subdued.

trajectory.position_description: Emotional life is integrated and quiet. He is repentant, grateful, affectionate, and ready for death.
key_moments: Wakes lucid after fever.
Confesses and makes his will.
Blesses Sancho.
Dies calmly.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Although stable delusion persists for most of the novel, the emotional register shifts from volatile self-righteousness to final resignation and calm.

relational_axes.axis_name: From instrumental command to affectionate reciprocal partnership
relational_axes.pole_start: Recruits Sancho with promises of an island and treats him as a subordinate, ignorant, cowardly, and a tool for witnessing and validating his madness; trust is high but esteem is low, and he punishes or threatens Sancho when contradicted.
relational_axes.pole_end: Depends on Sancho emotionally and practically, calls him friend and son, praises his natural wisdom, delegates judgment to him, stops his penance out of compassion, apologizes for leading him into madness, and rewards him in his will.

trajectory.position_description: The bond is hierarchical and transactional: Don Quixote promises rewards, ignores Sancho's warnings, treats him as an inferior witness, and punishes him when Sancho's mockery wounds his dignity.
key_moments: Persuades Sancho to become his squire with promises of an island.
Dismisses Sancho's warning about the windmills and about the friars.
Strikes Sancho after the fulling-mill humiliation.
Calls Sancho a fool and corrects his speech while relying on his reports.

trajectory.position_description: Conflict and dependence coexist: he beats or threatens Sancho over Dulcinea and the lashes, yet increasingly relies on his reports, care, and companionship.
key_moments: Sends Sancho to Dulcinea with the letter.
Beats Sancho for disparaging Dulcinea.
Refuses Sancho's demand for fixed wages and threatens to find another squire.
Reconciles tearfully with Sancho before the third sally and calls him friend and son.

trajectory.position_description: He recognizes Sancho's worth more often, calls him friend, grieves his absence during the governorship, and writes paternal counsel.
key_moments: Sends Sancho to El Toboso as his trusted intermediary to Dulcinea.
Warmly welcomes Sancho for the third sally.
Writes a paternal letter to Sancho as governor.
Praises Sancho's natural wisdom and defends him from mockery.

trajectory.position_description: The bond is tested by Sancho's governorship, separation, and return. Don Quixote writes affectionately, rescues Sancho from the pit, and values his counsel.
key_moments: Writes to Sancho as friend.
Rescues Sancho from the pit.
Leaves the castle with Sancho.
Accepts Sancho's truthful testimony over the garters.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat he becomes openly dependent and tender; he stops Sancho's whipping, values his judgment, apologizes for the whole knight-errantry venture, and provides for him.
key_moments: Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out in pain.
Delegates judgment to Sancho at the village wager.
Asks Sancho's forgiveness and cancels his debts in the final will.
Blesses Sancho, regrets leading him into madness, and wishes he could give him a kingdom.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The master-squire relationship moves from command and punishment toward trust, respect, emotional dependence, and final apology, making it the novel's central relational transformation.

relational_axes.axis_name: From self-authored ideal to anxious rescue fantasy and final relinquishment
relational_axes.pole_start: Constructs Aldonza as Dulcinea, Lady of Thoughts, the sovereign lady and judge of all deeds; devotion is literary, self-ornamental, and confirms his knightly identity rather than responding to a real relationship.
relational_axes.pole_end: The ideal becomes a persecuted enchanted lady whose rescue organizes his life; after his recovery of reason he renounces the chivalric frame that sustained her, abandoning the Dulcinea-enchantment quest and pastoral fantasy built around her, with no continuing relation to Aldonza depicted.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is invented to complete his knightly self: she is an abstract princess, judge, and motive for deeds, not a person he knows.
key_moments: Selects Aldonza Lorenzo and reinvents her as Dulcinea del Toboso.
Sends vanquished foes to her.
Invokes Dulcinea in combat, penance, and romance monologue.

trajectory.position_description: He admits he has rarely seen Aldonza and invents Dulcinea in imagination, yet still defends her supremacy with violence and devotional rhetoric.
key_moments: Tells Sancho that Dulcinea is really Aldonza but that he pictures her as an exalted princess.
Admits poets invent ladies and that he imagines Dulcinea.
Strikes Sancho for insulting Dulcinea.
Corrects Sancho's description of Dulcinea's eyes and mole to preserve her perfection.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea becomes the center of a disenchantment quest. After the El Toboso disillusion he insists she has been enchanted and treats Sancho's lashes as the necessary remedy.
key_moments: Sees a peasant girl on an ass as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Reports seeing the enchanted Dulcinea in the cave of Montesinos.
Vows to roam the earth until Dulcinea is disenchanted.
Accepts the staged Merlin's demand that Sancho whip himself for her release.

trajectory.position_description: Even after defeat, Dulcinea's disenchantment remains his central hope. He scans the road for her and ties his redemption to Sancho's fake lashes.
key_moments: Rejoices at the enchanted head's promise of Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Watches the road for Dulcinea after Sancho completes the lashes.
Counts the fake lashes on his rosary.
Sees omens that he will never see her.

trajectory.position_description: With the collapse of his chivalric identity, the enchantment project and pastoral fantasy around Dulcinea are discarded as part of his former illusion.
key_moments: Renounces books of chivalry.
Abandons knight-errantry and its Dulcinea project.
Dies as Alonso Quixano rather than as Dulcinea's knight.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea is the most intense object of Don Quixote's imaginative devotion, but the relationship is one-sided and literary; it intensifies into a rescue obsession and then fades as the chivalric worldview collapses.

relational_axes.axis_name: From impatient evasion to tender familial reconciliation
relational_axes.pole_start: He dismisses their warnings, secrets his plans, rebukes his niece for criticizing chivalry, and leaves home despite their distress, treating the household as an obstacle to his sallies.
relational_axes.pole_end: He calls them his daughters, reassures them, accepts their care in illness, protects his niece's inheritance from chivalry books in his will, and dies under their household care.

trajectory.position_description: The household is an obstacle to his sallies: he hides his plans, dismisses their fears, and treats their anti-chivalric concerns as ignorance or blasphemy.
key_moments: Accepts the housekeeper and niece's story of an enchanter taking his library.
Threatens his niece for calling chivalry histories fables.
Departs secretly or despite the niece's lamentation.

trajectory.position_description: Brief lucid conversation raises their hopes, but he reasserts knight-errantry and treats domestic opposition as a failure to understand his calling.
key_moments: Speaks so sensibly that the curate and barber hope he is cured.
Insists he will die a knight-errant.
Dismisses the housekeeper's threat to complain to the king.

trajectory.position_description: Weakened and finally sane, he becomes affectionate and dependent, addressing the women as daughters and accepting their care.
key_moments: Calls his niece and housekeeper his daughters and reassures them of his care.
Asks to be helped to bed because he does not feel well.
Makes a will protecting his niece's inheritance from chivalry books.
Dies under their household care.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The domestic relationship shifts from evasive rebellion against family concern to tender dependence and reconciliation in illness and death.

matched.set_a_axis: From dependent communion to self-asserting interdependence (Agency–communion balance)
matched.set_b_axis: From ambitious self-assertion to humble interdependence (Agency vs communion)
matched.overlap_description: Both treat Sancho's arc as movement along an agency/communion axis toward a mature mingling of self-assertion and loyalty. They DISAGREE on polarity: A says he starts at the communion/dependence pole (reward-seeking follower) and gains agency; B says he starts at the agency pole (mastery-seeking ambition) and gains communion. In practice his start is both reward-dependent and self-assertively ambitious, and both converge on an end state of interdependence.

matched.set_a_axis: From credulous chivalric belief to pragmatic skepticism (Credulity vs skepticism)
matched.set_b_axis: From credulous hope to disillusioned pragmatism (Credulity to empiricism)
matched.overlap_description: Near-identical: both trace Sancho from belief in islands, balsam, and chivalric truth toward practical skepticism/empiricism that tests claims against bodily experience, with residual enchantment-talk retained.

matched.set_a_axis: From grand political ambition to chastened domestic materialism (Ambition vs contentment)
matched.set_b_axis: From status aspiration to humble self-acceptance (Status self-perception)
matched.overlap_description: Both cover the inflation and puncturing of status ambition (island/county/governor/king) and a withdrawal toward modest domestic sufficiency. B emphasizes self-image ('Sancho Panza' over titles); A emphasizes the ambition→contentment value shift.

matched.set_a_axis: From opportunistic self-interest to conscience-guarded pragmatism (Self-interest vs conscience)
matched.set_b_axis: From transactional self-interest to conscientious mercy (Moral reasoning)
matched.overlap_description: Both describe a moral arc from spoils-and-bargain opportunism toward a conscience (honest government, refusing Ricote's bribe, clean hands) while noting residual comic deception (faked lashes).

unique_to_a.axis: From self-deprecating deference to self-respecting assertion (Self-dignity and assertion)

matched.set_a_axis: From hopeful trust to disillusioned ambivalence (Trust in judgment, Quixote)
matched.set_b_axis: From credulous deference to disillusioned devotion (Trust in judgment, Quixote)
matched.overlap_description: Same axis on trust in Quixote's judgment falling from credulity to open skepticism. B folds the accompanying devotion into this single axis; A keeps devotion as a separate axis.

matched.set_a_axis: From transactional service to deep affectionate devotion (Affectionate loyalty, Quixote)
matched.set_b_axis: From credulous deference to disillusioned devotion (devotion component, Quixote)
matched.overlap_description: A treats the loyalty/affection deepening as its own axis; B embeds it inside its single Quixote axis. Same underlying movement from reward-driven service to devoted attachment.

matched.set_a_axis: From hopeful provider to tested affectionate partnership (Marital partnership, Teresa)
matched.set_b_axis: From patronizing ambition to tender partnership (Marital intimacy and respect, Teresa)
matched.overlap_description: Both trace the marriage from instrumental/status-project framing (leaving without farewell, imagining Teresa a countess, teasing/autocratic) to tender, proud, companionate love (letters, acorns, 'Teresona').

matched.set_a_axis: From grateful awe to wary disillusionment (Trust in patrons, Duke and Duchess)
matched.set_b_axis: From grateful awe to wary disillusionment (Patron trust vs exploitation, Duke and Duchess)
matched.overlap_description: Essentially identical: awe and gratitude at ducal favor giving way to awareness of staged mockery, starvation, and humiliation during Barataria, with continued outward deference.

unique_to_a.axis: Affectionate loyalty to Quixote as a separate axis (rel_02)

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From dependent ambition to self-asserting interdependence
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Sancho enters service as a reward-seeking laborer who defines his worth through a patron's promises, defers to Quixote, imagines elevation to governor or king, treats the bond as a contract, and sets few boundaries over his labor or body.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He asserts bodily, economic, and moral boundaries, negotiates, governs and resigns, claims to be 'my own lord,' yet chooses loyal, affectionate interdependence with Quixote and his family rather than either pure dependence or pure self-interest.

trajectory.position_description: He leaves home for a promised island, treats service as a bargain, imagines himself as governor and his wife as queen, yet remains utterly dependent on Quixote's promises for worth.
key_moments: Leaves wife and children for the promised island
Reminds Quixote of the governorship after the battle
Defends Quixote's truthfulness while privately doubting Dulcinea

trajectory.position_description: He begins refusing suicidal combat and dangerous remedies, tallies his losses, demands concrete wages, protects his body and property, and privately resolves to go home.
key_moments: Refuses to fight commoners and declares himself a peaceable family man
Curses the balsam after it nearly kills him
Demands wages rather than vague promises and plans to leave

trajectory.position_description: He steers Quixote through cunning and fabrication, pushes the Micomicona marriage and a county, and asserts grievances while remaining tethered by intimacy and dependence.
key_moments: Fabricates the Dulcinea letter report to manage Quixote
Defends his spoils by force and insists he is no thief
Boasts at home of future office while admitting adventures end badly

trajectory.position_description: He sets conditions for service, bargains over wages, feels replaceable, then tearfully recommits; he publicly defends his own judgment and material interests.
key_moments: Wage demand refused; feels replaceable
Tearfully recommits after fearing replacement
Declares 'I stick to Camacho' and expounds a Haves/Haven'ts philosophy

trajectory.position_description: He exercises authority as governor, asserts his dignity against mockery, then renounces office and chooses simple freedom and loyal service.
key_moments: Judges the cane case and is hailed as a Solomon
Is starved by Doctor Recio and trampled in the mock assault
Renounces the governorship, saying he entered naked and leaves naked

trajectory.position_description: He refuses coerced penance yet remains at Quixote's deathbed, exercising agency within deep relational loyalty.
key_moments: Refuses the Dulcinea whipping as 'trick upon trick'
Stays at the bedside and begs Quixote not to die
Accepts Quixote's public praise and bequest

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho moves from a dependent, reward-seeking and status-ambitious follower to a self-asserting companion who negotiates, refuses, governs, resigns, and still chooses affectionate service. Both analyses agree the endpoint is interdependence—agency exercised within loyalty—rather than either pure independence or continued dependence.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From credulous chivalric belief to pragmatic empiricism
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He believes in the promised island or county, Quixote's chivalric explanations, magical remedies like the balsam, and the grand Dulcinea narrative.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He judges by practical evidence and bodily experience, openly doubts Quixote's sanity, rejects omens and grand promised rewards, though he still uses enchantment language tactically and retains an appetite for fantasy.

trajectory.position_description: He accepts the island promise and values magical shortcuts as concrete rewards, trusting Quixote as a man of quality.
key_moments: Believes Quixote will make him governor
Renounces the island temporarily for the balsam recipe's profit
Doubts Dulcinea privately but defends Quixote's general truthfulness

trajectory.position_description: Beatings, the balsam's effects, and Quixote's rage teach him that chivalric remedies and judgments are unreliable.
key_moments: The balsam nearly kills him and he curses it
Is struck for mocking the fulling mills and self-censors afterward
Says squires 'sup sorrow' while knights get glory

trajectory.position_description: He gains money but sees the Micomicona fiction collapse; skepticism about grand promised rewards hardens even as hope briefly revives.
key_moments: Admits he wept because Dorothea was not really Queen Micomicona
Openly accuses the curate and barber of staged trickery
Argues that enchanted people do not eat, drink, or answer questions

trajectory.position_description: He fabricates Dulcinea's enchantment, concludes Quixote is mad, and uses enchantment tactically to protect his own lie.
key_moments: Passes off peasant girls as Dulcinea and her damsels
Concludes Quixote is stark mad after the cave story
Feels vindicated when the ape says the cave story was partly false

trajectory.position_description: He judges office by experience, rejects omens, and sees Quixote's madness clearly, though a residual appetite for fantasy persists at the deathbed.
key_moments: Calls ambition misery and prefers his simple trade after office fails
Dismisses omens and buys the cricket cage to break them
Still clings briefly to the possibility of Dulcinea's disenchantment at the deathbed

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's arc is a long education in practical empiricism. He begins as a credulous believer in islands, balsam, and chivalric truth; by the end he regularly judges Quixote mad and trusts his senses, even if some convenient enchantment-talk and fantasy survive.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From grand political ambition to chastened self-accepting contentment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He treats an island, county, or title as the goal of service, imagines himself governor and his family elevated, studies courtly manners, and is willing to endure hardship for future elevation.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He declares himself unfit for governing, prefers 'Sancho Panza' and simple freedom to titles, renounces further office, and values family, food, and modest honestly-earned wealth—though he remains money-minded and status-aware.

trajectory.position_description: He imagines himself governor and his wife a countess or queen, expands ambition to county, kingdom, and emperorship, and studies how to behave as a count.
key_moments: Leaves home for the promised island and reminds Quixote of it
Imagines becoming a count and advises choosing a seacoast for his kingdom
Prays Quixote becomes emperor rather than archbishop

trajectory.position_description: The princess fiction collapses, his promised reward is exposed as illusion, yet he continues to plan for a county and a noble marriage for his daughter.
key_moments: Admits his tears were for lost profit
Eagerly claims the county and plans to farm its revenues
Insists he will make Mari-Sancha a countess, then postpones the plan to console Teresa

trajectory.position_description: He becomes puffed up before and during the governorship, boasts of being a 'principal personage' in print, and governs Barataria with confidence.
key_moments: Receives the governorship of Barataria
Boasts of being a famous figure in the printed history
Threatens Doctor Recio and asserts magisterial authority

trajectory.position_description: Hunger, fear, and humiliation teach him office exceeds his shoulders; he renounces Barataria and reclaims his ordinary identity.
key_moments: Is starved by Doctor Recio and terrified by the mock battle
Renounces the governorship, saying he entered and left naked
Says he is no good for governing except a drove of cattle

trajectory.position_description: He refuses further government and Ricote's bribe, returns home with money, values simple sufficiency and family while still relishing material gain and fame.
key_moments: Refuses 200 crowns rather than betray the king
Says he would not govern the whole world
Defends the money he brings home as honestly earned

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's ambition is repeatedly inflated, punctured, and recalibrated. By the end he has abandoned political rule but not material concern, producing a chastened, self-accepting domestic contentment rather than pure renunciation—while still enjoying being the famous true Sancho.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-deprecating deference to self-respecting assertion
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He accepts low status, calls himself simple or an ass, hides shame, and measures his worth by others' nobility and promises.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He defends his name, honesty, family honor, and real identity, insists he is no thief, and claims dignity as Sancho Panza even without letters or noble blood.

trajectory.position_description: He is credulous and self-deprecating, doubting whether his wife or he deserve elevation and preferring practical freedom to courtly honor.
key_moments: Doubts his wife's fitness to be queen
Prefers practical freedom to courtly honor

trajectory.position_description: Blanketing and humiliation make him avoid the inn that shamed him, though he asserts commoner honor when angry.
key_moments: Is blanketed at the inn
Refuses to enter the inn that shamed him
Insists he is 'a clown like myself' with a right to satisfaction

trajectory.position_description: He fights accusations of theft, learns he is in a published history, and insists on respectful treatment as an old Christian.
key_moments: Punches the barber and denies being a highwayman
Guards his reputation in the printed history
Defends spending the hundred crowns on his family

trajectory.position_description: As governor he asserts authority, resists mockery, and leaves office with a clear conscience and integrity.
key_moments: Rejects the title 'Don Sancho'
Rebukes Doctor Recio and delivers an admired speech
Renounces office without shame

trajectory.position_description: He denies theft, defends his true identity against impostors, and insists on his own worth and honesty.
key_moments: Indignantly denies stealing the garters
Rejects the false history's caricature of him
Declares himself the real Sancho Panza and defends his drollery

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho begins as a self-doubting rustic and ends as a man who publicly defends his name, honesty, and identity. His dignity grows through shame, office, and confrontations with mockery—a distinct dimension from political ambition that Set B folded into its status axis.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From opportunistic self-interest to conscience-guarded moral reasoning
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: He grabs spoils, hides windfalls, fabricates to manage Quixote, and measures actions by immediate material advantage.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He still acts pragmatically and sometimes deceptively, but increasingly governs with mercy and honesty, values a clear conscience, and refuses clearly corrupt gain while retaining comic lapses.

trajectory.position_description: He treats service as a bargain, seeks spoils, keeps found money, and invents the Dulcinea report to secure advantage.
key_moments: Tries to strip the fallen friar and is beaten
Keeps the valise's gold with delight and conceals it
Fabricates the Dulcinea letter delivery

trajectory.position_description: He lies to protect himself and manage Quixote, ties spoils and wages to legitimate service and family need, while showing flashes of compassion.
key_moments: Stages the enchanted Dulcinea fraud
Claims the pack-saddle as fair war spoils and the hundred crowns as earned
Shows brief charity to Andres

trajectory.position_description: In office he unexpectedly governs with practical mercy, protects the poor, punishes fraud, and renounces office with clean hands.
key_moments: Judges cases by evidence and draws up ordinances protecting the poor
Declares he will govern without bribes
Renounces office without profit after the mock assault

trajectory.position_description: He refuses Ricote's bribe and insists he is no thief, but later fakes the lashes for money—conscience real but not absolute.
key_moments: Refuses 200 crowns rather than betray the king
Accepts being thought a fool rather than a thief
Pretends to whip himself and lashes trees for payment

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's moral arc is mixed but real: he moves from casual opportunism toward a conscience that refuses obvious betrayal and values honest rule, while retaining pragmatic deception when he feels exploited or vulnerable.

relational_axes.axis_name: From hopeful trust to disillusioned, unsentimental ambivalence
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho trusts Quixote's chivalric promises and judgment, defends him against mockery, and expects the island through him.
relational_axes.pole_end: Sancho trusts Quixote's personal goodness but not his judgment: he sees him as mad, repeatedly deceives and manages him, and regards his chivalric promises with wary disbelief.

trajectory.position_description: He believes Quixote's promises and defends his truthfulness against strangers, treating the island as a serious contract.
key_moments: Trusts Quixote's island promise and accepts deferred reward
Defends Quixote while privately doubting the Dulcinea story

trajectory.position_description: Beatings, balsam poisoning, and wage disputes make him doubt Quixote's practical judgment while he still largely obeys.
key_moments: Is cudgeled after following Quixote
Curses the balsam and blames Quixote's broken oath for misfortunes
Demands concrete wages and plans to go home

trajectory.position_description: He openly calls the promised rewards wind and lies, sees the Micomicona scheme collapse, yet manages and deceives Quixote while remaining loyal.
key_moments: Calls the rewards 'wind and lies'
Admits his tears were for lost profit
Contradicts Quixote about the basin and is berated for an unwelcome truth

trajectory.position_description: Wage conflict, the Dulcinea deception, and the cave story convince him Quixote is unreliable and sometimes mad; trust in judgment is low but dependence and affection remain high.
key_moments: Wage demand is refused and he feels replaceable
Stages the enchanted Dulcinea to manipulate Quixote
Concludes Quixote is stark mad after the cave story

trajectory.position_description: After defeat and death he honors Quixote's goodness while no longer trusting his chivalric judgment.
key_moments: Sees his hopes collapse after Quixote's defeat
Comforts him as a 'great philosopher'
Accepts Quixote's apology and praise at the end

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's trust in Quixote's judgment erodes from chapter 16 onward, peaks in open skepticism during the Micomicona and cave episodes, and ends as affectionate but unsentimental wariness. Both sets agree the belief is lost without being replaced by renewed confidence in his judgment—only by affection on a separate axis.

relational_axes.axis_name: From transactional service to deep affectionate devotion
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho serves Quixote mainly for promised reward, with loyalty conditioned on the island and wages.
relational_axes.pole_end: Sancho's loyalty becomes deeply personal: he defends, rescues, mourns, prefers Quixote's company to any island, and stays at his deathbed even after renouncing the rewards.

trajectory.position_description: His bond is hopeful and reward-driven, conditioned on the promised island.
key_moments: Joins for the island
Asks for reward after the battle

trajectory.position_description: He resents beatings but still cares for the battered Quixote and is comforted by his promises.
key_moments: Helps the beaten Quixote and leads him to shelter
Is comforted by Quixote's promise of ass-colts

trajectory.position_description: He physically defends Quixote, plans escapes, and grieves when he thinks Quixote dead.
key_moments: Rushes to defend Quixote from Cardenio
Is called 'brother Sancho'
Delivers a tearful lament over Quixote's body

trajectory.position_description: After the wage quarrel he tearfully recommits, tells Quixote he loves him, and defends him publicly.
key_moments: Retracts wage demands and reconciles
Says he loves Quixote as the core of his heart
Defends Quixote's honor

trajectory.position_description: As governor he is separated but homesick and loyal; after renouncing office he returns to Quixote.
key_moments: Admits homesickness in his letter
Is rescued by Quixote from the pit
Formally returns to Quixote's service

trajectory.position_description: He stays with Quixote through illness and death, showing devotion beyond reward.
key_moments: Never leaves the bedside and begs him not to die
Mourns Quixote's death

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Although Sancho's loyalty begins as a reward contract, it becomes genuinely affectionate. He repeatedly rescues, defends, mourns, prefers Quixote's company to any island, and finally attends him in death—rising even as his trust in Quixote's judgment falls.

relational_axes.axis_name: From patronizing ambition to tender companionate partnership
relational_axes.pole_start: He leaves Teresa without farewell and treats her as a beneficiary and instrument of his rise, imagining her a countess mainly as part of his own elevation and occasionally patronizing or autocratic toward her.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends tender, proud, and companionate, valuing Teresa's virtue, letters, and domestic life over titles, affirming deep love while still teasing and money-conscious.

trajectory.position_description: He leaves without farewell and thinks of Teresa as a beneficiary of his rise, doubting her fitness for a crown.
key_moments: Leaves wife and children without farewell
Imagines Teresa as a countess
Doubts she is worth two maravedis as a queen

trajectory.position_description: He is affectionate but autocratic, promises Teresa a ladyship, quarrels over Sanchica's countesshood, then consoles her.
key_moments: Tells Teresa she will soon be a ladyship despite having no wages
Dismisses Teresa's warnings about inequality
Postpones the countess plan to comfort her

trajectory.position_description: Separation makes his affection more explicit; he sends gifts and letters, weeps over her replies, and praises her honesty.
key_moments: Sends Sanchica his suit and shares it with the household
Weeps over Teresa's letters and acorns
Praises her acorns as gratitude rather than bribery

trajectory.position_description: He returns with money and renewed domestic loyalty, names her affectionately, and defends his honest provision and love for her.
key_moments: Says he loves Teresa better than his own eyelids
Insists he brings honestly earned money
Receives Quixote's bequest and returns to family life

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The marriage is not static: it is strained by Sancho's ambition and social climbing, softened by his affection, gifts, and letters, and finally grounded in his return as a loving provider. His attitude shifts from using Teresa as part of a status fantasy to tender, proud, companionate attachment.

relational_axes.axis_name: From grateful awe to wary disillusionment
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho is delighted and grateful for noble recognition, gifts, and the promised governorship, trusting the Duke and Duchess as generous benefactors and confiding in them.
relational_axes.pole_end: He remains outwardly deferential and grateful for gifts, but has experienced their mockery, manipulation, and starvation of him in office, so his trust becomes wary and conditional.

trajectory.position_description: He is charmed and flattered by noble recognition, quotes himself, and trusts the Duke and Duchess's promises, unaware of the staged amusement.
key_moments: The Duchess welcomes him as a known figure from print
Confides his Dulcinea deception to the Duchess
The Duke confers the governorship

trajectory.position_description: He remains trusting but is repeatedly frightened and manipulated by staged spectacles, clinging to ducal protection.
key_moments: Receives the green hunting suit
Faints onto the Duchess's robe during the night spectacle
Trusts the Duke's reassurance about the island

trajectory.position_description: Office becomes starvation and intrigue; he suspects Doctor Recio and resents the Duke's arrangement, renouncing the government though still respectful.
key_moments: Is starved at the banquet
Curses the government and the one who gave it
Is trampled in the mock alarm and renounces the governorship

trajectory.position_description: He leaves with gifts and gratitude but now understands the court's power to mock and manipulate him.
key_moments: Accepts the majordomo's purse but resents staged humiliations
Refuses to be used as Altisidora's remedy
Calls the duennas' smacks the worst insult

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's relationship with the Duke and Duchess moves from enchanted gratitude to experienced wariness. He does not break with them, but he has learned that their favor can be theatrical, controlling, and humiliating—awareness without outright rupture.

matched.set_a_axis: Agency–Communion (attributed)
matched.set_b_axis: Agency–Communion Objecthood
matched.overlap_description: Both track Dulcinea's status as an object of projection with no independent agency or reciprocal communion, from a nominal sovereign/object to a staged mouthpiece/erased referent. Both note the flat intrapsychic arc due to lack of interiority.

matched.set_a_axis: Testimonial trust
matched.set_b_axis: Fraudulent Dependence
matched.overlap_description: Both track Sancho's role from trusted envoy/familiar witness to confessed fabricator and unpaid debtor, with trust destroyed and replaced by fraudulent dependence.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Nominal Sovereign to Staged Mouthpiece: agency remains counterfeit, communion remains unilateral
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A pure object of Don Quixote's projective communion, invented as a lady with no independent agency or reciprocal relational warmth; her 'agency' is grammatical only.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Still a relational object, never an agent; her one apparent agentic scene (the ducal masque) is ventriloquized, and by the end even her objecthood dissolves into pastoral pretext and omission from Quixote's dying words.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea exists as an invoked name in prefatory verse and then as Quixote's fabrication laid over Aldonza Lorenzo. She initiates nothing and reciprocates nothing; her 'agency' is grammatical only.
key_moments: Chapter 1: named in commendatory verse as an absent lady.
Chapter 2: invented by Quixote as a name 'musical, uncommon, and significant.'
Chapter 3: invoked as scornful princess who 'drove him forth.'
Chapter 6: renamed into borrowed literary fictions such as Xarifa.

trajectory.position_description: Her name acquires operative force: prayed to before combat, used as legal receipt, destination for defeated men, forged in letters. Agency belongs entirely to Quixote, Sancho, the curate, and the barber.
key_moments: Chapter 11: Sancho uses her name as a brake on Quixote's oath.
Chapter 21: Quixote commends himself to her beside God before the fulling hammers.
Chapter 23: freed convicts refuse the errand to El Toboso and commute it to Ave Marias.
Chapter 26: Quixote admits he pictures her as he would have her be.
Chapter 28: the curate invents a command in her name.
Chapter 31: Sancho confesses the embassy was invented.
Chapter 32: Sancho invents a laughing Dulcinea and a torn letter.

trajectory.position_description: Her non-agency becomes explicit: letters undelivered or reconstructed, Sancho confesses he never truly saw her, Quixote concedes she may be imaginary. She is a destination, legal condition, and forgery, not a subject. Dorothea displaces her as addressee of knightly deeds.
key_moments: Chapter 31: Sancho confesses the embassy was invented.
Chapter 32: Sancho invents a laughing Dulcinea and a torn letter.
Chapter 47: she becomes a prophecy's cipher: white dove, womb, future whelps.
Chapter 49: her name is reduced to a conjuring formula Quixote silences.
Chapter 52: Leandra is given speech, desire, error, and consequence; Dulcinea is given none.
Chapter 61: Quixote forbids the wheat-sifting memory and relocates her to a palace.
Chapter 62: Quixote admits he loves her 'solely by hearsay.'

trajectory.position_description: She acquires a grave, a counterfeit peasant body, and finally a speaking role in the ducal masque. Yet every apparent act is authored by others: the epitaph by academicians, the peasant body by Sancho, the voice and tears by the duke and duchess.
key_moments: Chapter 53: an epitaph declares 'Here Dulcinea lies,' assigning her a death she never chose.
Chapter 61: El Toboso is reached, but she does not appear.
Chapter 63: Sancho stages a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Chapter 76: in the cave she flees and begs by proxy for six reals.
Chapter 84: Quixote publicly testifies she is enchanted into 'the most ill-favoured peasant wench'.
Chapter 85: the Duchess proposes she may be 'an imaginary lady'; belief in her becomes a household policy.
Chapter 88: she speaks in Merlin's masque, demanding Sancho's lashes.
Chapter 89: the masque is revealed as a ducal drollery; Merlin is a majordomo.

trajectory.position_description: She is almost wholly offstage: a postponed whipping, a curse, a pastoral name, an unpaid score. The fraudulent 'disenchantment' is announced without her presence, and Quixote's recovery of reason dissolves the world that housed her. She neither acts nor is granted a final word.
key_moments: Chapter 93: her disenchantment is scheduled for 'leisure hours.'
Chapter 103: Sancho is said to have forgotten the disenchantment entirely.
Chapter 110: Altisidora curses her to remain enchanted forever.
Chapter 113: attempted coerced flogging; sworn promise of voluntary penance; disenchantment deferred again.
Chapter 125: Sancho's lashes are counted against trees; her cure is declared accomplished by fraud.
Chapter 126: she becomes a pastoral pretext rather than a woman to be found.
Chapter 127: Quixote dies sane; Dulcinea is absent from his confession, will, and dying words.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea has no interiority in the text. On the agency–communion axis she never becomes an agent and never enters reciprocal communion; she is only the object of others' projections, errands, forgeries, and staged performances. The apparent 'voice' in Chapter 88 is counterfeit, so the arc remains flat.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Corporeal Neighbour to Vanished Referent: the erosion of Aldonza into a pure name
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A real, locatable person with body, labour, lineage and a loud voice — Aldonza Lorenzo, daughter of Lorenzo Corchuelo and Aldonza Nogales, who flings a crowbar, hackles flax, threshes grain and jokes with everybody (Sancho's testimony, ch26 and ch32).
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: A reputation with no verifiable referent: 'nothing in the world but an imaginary lady' (ch85), whose only documentary form by ch94 is the phrase 'white dove' on a placard, and whose existence is something a household agrees to 'believe.'

trajectory.position_description: Highest ontological solidity: Sancho names her family, her strength, her voice, her work. The ideal and the person are still visibly the same woman, and Quixote's refusal to let the facts alter the ideal is the first crack.
key_moments: Chapter 26: Sancho identifies her as Aldonza Lorenzo and describes her concretely; Quixote insists she is 'as good as the most exalted princess on earth'.

trajectory.position_description: Her paper existence is annihilated: the letter is torn unread, she can neither read nor write, no reply ever existed, and her messenger has never seen her. The narration states flatly that 'Dulcinea' has no empirical referent.
key_moments: Chapter 31: Sancho confesses he carried no letter and forgot the memorized text.
Chapter 32: invented embassy — wheat-sifting, illiteracy, cheese over the yard wall — which Quixote transfigures into pearls and Sabaean odour.
Chapter 32: 'Sancho knew Dulcinea to be a peasant girl... and had never seen her in all his life'.
Chapter 32: her silence is redefined as decorum, so her interiority need never be consulted.

trajectory.position_description: The referent dissolves at her own doorstep: Sancho's eyewitness wheat-sifting is classed as an enchanter's fraud, and Quixote admits he has never seen her house or her face. She is now constituted by circulating report.
key_moments: Chapter 61: the wheat-sifting is reclassified as diabolical distortion; she 'must have been' at needlework.
Chapter 62: 'enamoured solely by hearsay'; Sancho retracts his eyewitness claim.

trajectory.position_description: Her being becomes a proposition to be voted on: printed fame brings her to a ducal drawing room where she is called possibly imaginary, denied outright by a churchman, confessed a hoax by Sancho, and then re-imposed as true by ducal decree and staged pageantry.
key_moments: Chapter 83: the Duchess knows her from the printed First Part as a catalogue entry.
Chapter 84: the ecclesiastic names 'enchanted Dulcineas' among things that do not exist.
Chapter 85: 'an imaginary lady... begot in his own brain'; Quixote's counter-claim that she is 'the daughter of her own works'.
Chapter 86: Sancho confesses the enchantment was his invention — 'no more truth in it than over the hills of Úbeda'.
Chapter 86: the Duchess restores her reality by fiat.

trajectory.position_description: She survives only as inscription and memory: a placard's 'white dove,' and a remembered image of a country wench on a she-ass that Quixote cannot reconcile with the lady he worships.
key_moments: Chapter 94: Merlin's decree names her only as 'the white dove'.
Chapter 113: Quixote broods on her as last 'seen' in the cave, skipping on her ass.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The novel systematically subtracts every empirical warrant for her: no letter delivered, no reading, no reply, no sighting by her own envoy, no sighting even by her lover. What begins as a named peasant woman with a family and a threshing floor ends as a phrase on a lance and a thing a duchess promises to 'believe.' A flat interior arc — she never learns she is being invented — recorded as steady ontological erosion.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Doctrinal Chastity to Contested Costume: the ideal's moral authority deflating into performance
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Her virtue is unquestionable doctrine: she is incapable of betrayal, 'as the mother that bore her,' and her silence is decorous modesty that others must respect and never question.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Her virtue is legible as a role authored by men and worn like a costume — publicly mocked as 'prudery' by ordinary women, demonstrated as improvisable by Dorothea, doubted as a fiction by a duchess, and formally reduced to a squire's lie about pearls and wheat.

trajectory.position_description: Her chastity functions as a premise that forecloses any interior life and licenses speaking for her: modesty explains silence, and silence excuses the absence of consent.
key_moments: Chapter 27: her fidelity asserted as absolute, used to select Quixote's role.
Chapter 32: 'Dulcinea is so decorous that she does not wish her thoughts to be known'.

trajectory.position_description: Ordinary women judge the archetype heartless; Dorothea wears and drops queenship at will; the Moorish lady insists on her own name. The ideal is measured against living women and found to be a performance.
key_moments: Chapter 33: the landlord's daughter condemns 'cruel ladies' as pointless prudery — 'if it is for honour's sake, why not marry them?'
Chapter 38: Dorothea sustains and discards invented sovereignty to manage a madman.
Chapter 38: María's tearful insistence on her own name stands as a foil to Dulcinea's imposed one.

trajectory.position_description: Her virtue's authority becomes a debating point at court: her lineage is mocked, her existence doubted, her enchantment confessed a hoax, and her 'good name' legally injured by a squire's fabrication — then repaired only as a game.
key_moments: Chapter 85: the duke scorns her lineage; the duchess proposes 'belief' in her as a household policy.
Chapter 86: the duchess charges that Sancho's wheat-sifting report prejudiced 'the peerless Dulcinea's good name'.
Chapter 86: Sancho admits the enchantment was invented to escape a scolding.

trajectory.position_description: Her condition and her restoration are absorbed into a staged pageant with devils and triumphal cars: the ideal's moral seriousness is fully converted into aristocratic entertainment.
key_moments: Chapter 87: she is announced as enchanted cargo on a triumphal car, her remedy scripted by the duke and duchess.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: No inward moral change is possible for a character given no consciousness; what changes is the standing of the virtue she embodies. Quixote's decorum is successively translated by other women into prudery, by Dorothea into costume, by a duke into bad lineage and by a duchess into 'belief' — a doctrine becomes a performance. Confidence is medium because the axis is carried by the novel's surrounding commentary rather than by anything Dulcinea says or does.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Unwitting Construct to Unwitting Construct: self-knowledge never develops
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Dulcinea begins with no interiority, no beliefs of her own, and no awareness that she has been named, invented, or loved by hearsay.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: She ends exactly as unaware: she never learns that she is a fiction, never learns of Sancho's fraud, never learns that the disenchantment was staged, and never learns that Quixote's recovery of reason dissolves her. The text closes without granting her a single moment of self-recognition.

trajectory.position_description: She is a name and a fabricated beloved. The narrative never enters her, so self-awareness is not merely absent but structurally impossible.
key_moments: Chapter 2: Aldonza Lorenzo 'never knew it nor gave a thought to the matter.'
Chapter 10: her first concrete attribute is a marginal joke about salting pigs.
Chapter 14: Quixote admits he 'cannot say positively' whether she is pleased.
Chapter 26: she is identified as Aldonza Lorenzo, illiterate and unaware of Quixote's gaze.

trajectory.position_description: Facts accumulate around her—illiteracy, a letter she cannot read, forged commands, an epitaph—but none reaches her consciousness. Knowledge about her grows; her knowledge of herself does not.
key_moments: Chapter 27: Quixote appends 'del Toboso' and later admits the verse would be unintelligible without it.
Chapter 28: the curate supplies her with a forged command and confirms she cannot read.
Chapter 38: she survives only as the phrase 'his lady's scorn.'
Chapter 47: she is given a prophetic womb and future without being consulted.

trajectory.position_description: She receives a body, an epitaph, a counterfeit peasant double, and a speaking masque role, but she never knows that these are performances. Her apparent feelings are authored by others.
key_moments: Chapter 53: strangers bury her in verse and epitaph without her consent.
Chapter 63: a peasant girl is enthroned as her and speaks only to refuse.
Chapter 76: she flees from being addressed in the cave.
Chapter 88: she voices scripted grief and demands lashes from Sancho.
Chapter 89: the reader learns Merlin is the duke's majordomo; she never does.

trajectory.position_description: Her disenchantment is postponed, forgotten, fraudulently completed, and finally voided by Quixote's sanity. She never appears to learn any of it. The book ends without giving her a final scene or a moment of insight.
key_moments: Chapter 103: Sancho has 'forgotten all about' the disenchantment.
Chapter 110: Altisidora wishes her permanently enchanted.
Chapter 125: her cure is certified by lashes laid on trees.
Chapter 126: an omen says she will never be seen; the pastoral scheme replaces rescue with verse.
Chapter 127: Quixote dies sane and does not mention her in his will or final confession.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Across the summaries Dulcinea is repeatedly described as having no interiority, no beliefs, no desires, and no self-awareness. Even when she is given scripted speech and staged emotion, the text withholds any moment in which she knows herself or her situation. This axis is therefore flat by design.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Presumed Mutual Bond to Confessed Soliloquy
relational_axes.pole_start: An ostensibly reciprocal courtship: embassies are planned, letters written, a reply awaited, a love of twelve years' standing with four modest encounters behind it.
relational_axes.pole_end: An openly unilateral devotion: the lover confesses he has never seen her or crossed her threshold and loves her 'solely by hearsay,' while weeping over an enchanted peasant he cannot restore.

trajectory.position_description: The relation is treated by Quixote as a functioning bond with a real addressee; he plans to send her a verse letter and speaks of their modest glances as a shared history.
key_moments: Chapter 22: she is the standard against which Helen is measured.
Chapter 24: a verse letter to her is promised to Sancho as messenger.
Chapter 26: the four sightings in twelve years and the admission that he imagines her as he would have her be.

trajectory.position_description: Contact is simulated entirely: a forged spoken command, then a fabricated visit, an undelivered letter and an unread one. The correspondence that appeared to constitute intimacy is shown never to have existed.
key_moments: Chapter 28: a reply and a summons are authored for her.
Chapter 31: the letter was never carried; no reply can ever have existed.
Chapter 32: the invented embassy of wheat, sweat and cheese which Quixote transfigures into pearls.

trajectory.position_description: She is honoured as a clause, a battle-cry and an oracle while Quixote's obedience migrates to Micomicona; the relation is conducted in her name by others.
key_moments: Chapter 30: she becomes a legal reservation on the Micomicona boon.
Chapter 45: her name is absent entirely; permission is sought of Dorothea.
Chapter 47: a false prophecy of marriage and sons is read as her guarantee.

trajectory.position_description: At her own doorstep the fiction of reciprocity is dismantled by Quixote himself; the bond is declared to rest on reputation alone, and Sancho withdraws his corroboration.
key_moments: Chapter 61: her real employment is overruled as an enchanter's fraud.
Chapter 62: 'I have never seen her in my life... enamoured solely by hearsay'.

trajectory.position_description: Devotion reaches maximum intensity at maximum distance: he testifies publicly that she is enchanted into a hideous peasant, vows endless tears, and finally attempts to coerce Sancho's flogging to restore her.
key_moments: Chapter 84: he confesses she is 'turned into the most ill-favoured peasant wench'.
Chapter 85: 'daughter of her own works' — he defends her being rather than her person.
Chapter 113: attempted forced flagellation to end her enchantment fails; the rescue is deferred.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the novel's cleanest trackable relational decline: every apparent channel of contact (letter, messenger, forged reply, embassy, visit) is exposed as fabricated or void, and Quixote himself names the relation hearsay at ch62. The trajectory is one-directional — intimacy thins as rhetoric inflates — which is why confidence is high.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Celebrated Beauty to Militantly Defended Abstraction
relational_axes.pole_start: Esteem expressed as lyric celebration: her beauty is the measure of all beauty, her name a synonym for the peerless, offered freely and with pleasure.
relational_axes.pole_end: Esteem expressed as ideology under siege: she must be vindicated by blows, by forced confessions from rivals, by 'all comparisons are odious,' and by the assertion that her virtue 'rectifies blood' — worship as enforcement.

trajectory.position_description: Her superlative status is asserted for pleasure and ornament, requiring no defence because no one contests it.
key_moments: Chapter 22: Helen would not be so famous had Dulcinea lived then.
Chapter 27: her name becomes a verse refrain on tree bark.

trajectory.position_description: Esteem becomes combative for the first time: Sancho's comparison with Dorothea earns a beating, and her worth is declared the efficient cause of Quixote's valour.
key_moments: Chapter 31: Sancho says she is 'not half as fair' as Dorothea.
Chapter 31: 'she fights in me and conquers in me' — esteem converted to doctrine.
Chapter 32: every coarse detail alchemised into proof of perfection.

trajectory.position_description: His esteem must now survive his own reports of her degradation: an enchanter is blamed for the wheat, and he publicly testifies to her hideous peasant form while maintaining her peerlessness.
key_moments: Chapter 61: the wheat-sifting attributed to an envious enchanter.
Chapter 76: 'all comparisons are odious' — Montesinos must retract a comparison.
Chapter 84: peerless lady publicly confessed to be enchanted into a wench.

trajectory.position_description: Esteem is legalistic and defensive: she is defended against doubters as 'the daughter of her own works,' her lineage argued at a ducal table, and her standing finally pursued through a coerced flogging.
key_moments: Chapter 85: 'virtues rectify blood'; vow of ceaseless tears.
Chapter 86: ducal decree reinstates her beauty and eventual proper form.
Chapter 113: an attempted forced penance undertaken on her behalf.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The level of Quixote's esteem never falls — it is the *character* of that esteem that changes, from spontaneous lyric praise to a creed requiring violence, legal argument and ducal ratification. Confidence is medium because the shift is tonal and rhetorical rather than a change in rank on the dimension.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Sole Devotional Object to Dispensable Literary Pretext
relational_axes.pole_start: Dulcinea begins as Quixote's invented, singular lady: the absent beloved whose name licenses knight-errantry and whose imagined scorn or favor organizes his quest. She is relationally central, but entirely as an object of his devotion.
relational_axes.pole_end: She ends as a dissolved pretext. Quixote's recovery of reason folds her into the 'dark shadows' of his madness; he does not renounce her with contempt, but he omits her from his confession, will, and dying words. The relation is not broken by her but dissolved with the fiction that housed it.

trajectory.position_description: She is created in Quixote's mind and invoked in borrowed literary forms. Her centrality is absolute in rhetoric but abstract in fact.
key_moments: Chapter 2: Quixote invents Dulcinea as his lady.
Chapter 3: he calls her 'Princess Dulcinea' and accuses her of scorn.
Chapter 5: her beauty becomes an article of faith to be confessed without seeing her.
Chapter 6: she is renamed into the ballad and Moorish Xarifa.

trajectory.position_description: Her name is used to bless combat, judge defeated men, and serve as a legal receipt. Quixote's relation to her is functionally central but increasingly administrative.
key_moments: Chapter 9: he commends himself to her before the windmills and Biscayan.
Chapter 10: the Biscayan is sent to her as judge.
Chapter 11: Sancho uses her name to stop Quixote's oath.
Chapter 21: Quixote commends himself to her beside God.
Chapter 23: freed convicts are ordered to El Toboso and refuse.

trajectory.position_description: Quixote admits he pictures her as he would have her be, and her name is handled through forged letters, invented replies, and legal conditions. She remains central, but the relation is openly mediated by fraud and literary convention.
key_moments: Chapter 26: Quixote says, 'I picture her in my imagination as I would have her to be.'
Chapter 31: Sancho confesses the embassy was invented.
Chapter 32: Sancho invents a Dulcinea who laughs at the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
Chapter 47: Quixote decodes a prophecy into her womb and future sons.
Chapter 49: her name becomes a conjuration he silences.

trajectory.position_description: She becomes a problem to be solved: an epitaph, a searched-for address, a counterfeit peasant, and an enchantment to be undone. Quixote's devotion remains absolute, but it is increasingly directed at a condition rather than a person.
key_moments: Chapter 53: academicians bury her in epitaph.
Chapter 61: Quixote forbids the wheat-sifting memory and relocates her to a palace.
Chapter 63: he kneels to a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Chapter 64: he proposes an experiment to test who can see her.
Chapter 76: in the cave she flees from him and begs by proxy.

trajectory.position_description: Her cure becomes a ducal entertainment and then a negotiated payment in Sancho's lashes. Quixote defends her name, but his devotion becomes elegiac, pastoral, and finally fraudulent in its 'completion.'
key_moments: Chapter 85: Quixote concedes 'God knows whether there be any Dulcinea or not.'
Chapter 88: she appears in Merlin's masque demanding Sancho's lashes.
Chapter 110: Altisidora curses her to remain enchanted.
Chapter 117: Quixote is defeated while defending her beauty and bound to a year of peace.
Chapter 125: Sancho's tree-whipping is counted as her cure.

trajectory.position_description: She becomes a pastoral name to be carved on trees rather than a woman to be found. When Quixote recovers reason and dies, she is absent from his will and final words; the relation ends not by rejection but by the collapse of the fiction that sustained it.
key_moments: Chapter 126: Quixote plans a pastoral life and verse; an omen says Dulcinea will never be seen.
Chapter 127: Quixote says he was mad and is now sane; Dulcinea is omitted from his confession, will, and death.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The relation is trackable chiefly from Quixote's side, since Dulcinea has no reciprocal interiority. It moves from singular devotional object to legal/tribunal instrument, to enchantment problem, to theatrical/economic cipher, to final omission. Because her own attitude is never represented, confidence is medium.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Trusted Envoy to Confessed Fabricator and Unpaid Debtor
relational_axes.pole_start: He is her knowledgeable neighbour and appointed ambassador: he can name her parents, describe her strength and voice, and is trusted to carry a letter and return her reply.
relational_axes.pole_end: He is the confessed inventor of her enchantment and her wheat-sifting, whose word about her is worthless and whose last link to her is a debt of lashes he keeps deferring.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho uses Dulcinea's name as a limit on Quixote's behavior and as the destination of errands. He is functionally her courier and speaks of her with earthy affection and rough praise.
key_moments: Chapter 11: Sancho calls her 'my lady Dulcinea del Toboso' and uses her name to stop Quixote's oath.
Chapter 21: Sancho is designated her messenger in the event of Quixote's death.
Chapter 23: her errand is refused and converted into prayers.
Chapter 26: Sancho reveals her as Aldonza Lorenzo, a farm girl he knows.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes the chief fabricator of her responses: he loses the letter, reconstructs it from memory, invents her reply, and confesses he never truly viewed her. Her relation to him becomes mediated by forgery.
key_moments: Chapter 27: Sancho misremembers and reconstructs the letter.
Chapter 31: he confesses the embassy was invented and that he never saw her.
Chapter 32: he invents a Dulcinea who laughs and tears the letter.
Chapter 35: he admits he never saw her 'at my leisure.'

trajectory.position_description: Sancho stages a peasant girl as Dulcinea and invents her physical charms. Her 'body' in the text becomes his improvisation, while she remains unaware.
key_moments: Chapter 61: Sancho dreads locating her house in El Toboso.
Chapter 62: he confesses his earlier 'sighting' was hearsay.
Chapter 63: he presents a village girl as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Chapter 64: Quixote corrects Sancho's description of her eyes and teeth.

trajectory.position_description: Her disenchantment becomes dependent on Sancho's lashes. He refuses, evades, and treats the debt as an imposition, while the ducal masque turns her demand into a staged coercion of his body.
key_moments: Chapter 70: Quixote commends himself to her before the lions and makes Sancho her legatee.
Chapter 76: she flees in the cave while Sancho laughs at his own invention.
Chapter 88: the masque-Dulcinea demands 3,300 lashes from Sancho.
Chapter 89: Sancho gives himself only five strokes with his bare hand.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho converts her release into a transaction, haggles over the price, and finally 'pays' by whipping trees. Her cure is fraudulently completed in name while she remains absent. He remains the only character still promising her restoration, but his promise is a habit of fidelity to Quixote rather than a working cure.
key_moments: Chapter 93: he postpones her whipping to 'leisure hours.'
Chapter 103: he is said to have forgotten the disenchantment.
Chapter 124: he haggles at 825 reals and whips beech trees.
Chapter 125: he claims to be 'very well whipped'; Quixote counts the fraud as triumph.
Chapter 126: Sancho turns an omen into a joke and presses a hare into Quixote's arms as Dulcinea.
Chapter 127: Sancho promises they may find Dulcinea disenchanted behind a bush; Quixote declines the fantasy and dies sane.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Trust is measurably destroyed by explicit authorial statement: the narrator flatly reports that Sancho 'had never seen her in all his life,' and Sancho later confesses the enchantment and the wheat-sifting were his inventions. What survives is not testimony but a transactional debt. Confidence high because the disclosures are overt and dated.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Earthy Affection to Fluctuating Comparison
relational_axes.pole_start: Esteem grounded in concrete familiarity: a strong, loud, funny woman he has known all his life and praises for real qualities.
relational_axes.pole_end: Esteem expressed only as a comparative ranking that swings with circumstance — demoted below Dorothea, equated with the Duchess, restored to 'fairest creature in the world' when it suits a defence.

trajectory.position_description: He values her as a person he knows: her crowbar-throw, her voice from the belfry, her joking.
key_moments: Chapter 26: the farm-girl description offered as rough affection.

trajectory.position_description: He measures her against Dorothea and finds her wanting, then reduces her to a caricature of sweat and cheese in the very act of praising her industry.
key_moments: Chapter 31: 'not half as fair' — publicly demoted from peerless.
