Chapter 32: the winnowing, illiterate, cheese-giving peasant of his invention.

trajectory.position_description: Her rank is again set by comparison — equated with the Duchess, then asserted as supreme in a court that has just called her enchanted and hideous.
key_moments: Chapter 83: 'the Duchess is in no way behind her'.
Chapter 84: 'the fairest creature in the world' — leaping onto an ass like a cat.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Esteem is real but volatile and entirely comparative; it moves from the texture of acquaintance to the arithmetic of ranking, losing all content beyond 'fairer' or 'not so fair.' Confidence medium because the oscillation could also be read as constant, merely inarticulate, affection.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Unwitting Usurper to Self-Styled Servant: homage as erasure
relational_axes.pole_start: A stranger who, costumed as a princess in distress, takes over the functional role of the lady who commands knightly service — without ever knowing Dulcinea's name.
relational_axes.pole_end: The usurper publicly styles herself Dulcinea's servant and well-wisher, a deference that seals rather than repairs the displacement, since she commands the oath and the knees.

trajectory.position_description: Dorothea receives the boon, the vow and the service that Dulcinea's name had formerly commanded, and is openly judged the fairer of the two.
key_moments: Chapter 30: the Micomicona boon displaces her as addressee of knightly deeds.
Chapter 31: Sancho measures them and finds Dorothea superior.

trajectory.position_description: Dorothea declares herself Dulcinea's servant and prays for her behalf while occupying the saddle and the story; her own queenship is shown to be a costume she can wear and drop.
key_moments: Chapter 31: 'I know nothing of that lady Toboso save that she is her servant'.
Chapter 38: invented sovereignty worn and re-worn at will, undercutting Dulcinea's imagined rank.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The axis is one of structural antagonism without contact: Dorothea performs the lady-function more effectively than the lady herself and cheapens aristocratic identity in the process. Confidence medium because the rivalry is never acknowledged by either woman.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Printed Name to Staged Spectacle
relational_axes.pole_start: A name the Duchess knows only from the printed First Part — a catalogue entry in another man's story, discussed as a curiosity.
relational_axes.pole_end: A theatrical property: the Duchess pledges household-wide 'belief' in her, reinstates her enchantment as fact, and stages her triumphal arrival in a pageant of devils and cars.

trajectory.position_description: She enters the Duchess's world as literary reputation; the Duchess asks for trophies and treats her as a fixture of a story to be played with.
key_moments: Chapter 83: 'a certain Dulcinea del Toboso' — the name confirmed from print.
Chapter 84: the Duchess asks what presents of vanquished giants she has lately received.

trajectory.position_description: The Duchess proposes that Dulcinea may be imaginary, then converts belief in her into an amused decree, and finally re-imposes the enchantment as authoritative truth after Sancho's confession.
key_moments: Chapter 85: 'an imaginary lady... begot in his own brain'; promise that all her household will 'believe'.
Chapter 86: 'knowledge from good authority' that the wench on the ass is Dulcinea, enchanted through no fault of her own.

trajectory.position_description: Her condition and her cure are absorbed into a ducal spectacle: she is announced as enchanted cargo on a triumphal car, delivered to Quixote for instruction.
key_moments: Chapter 87: a demon-courier announces her arrival; her fate is scripted entirely by the ducal pair.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the sharpest late-stage relational change: a stranger acquires near-total authorial control over Dulcinea's public being — deciding whether she exists, whether she is enchanted, and how she shall appear. Confidence high because the Duchess's interventions are explicit, sequential and self-consciously theatrical.

matched.set_a_axis: From manipulative self-assertion to relational stewardship
matched.set_b_axis: From Self-Aggrandizing Agency to Genial Communal Embeddedness
matched.overlap_description: Both axes track Carrasco's movement from instrumental, self-aggrandizing social agency toward greater communal participation, while noting that his warmth remains patronizing.

matched.set_a_axis: From illusion of engineered control to chastened acceptance of limits
matched.set_b_axis: From Confident Manipulative Cure to Baffled Denial of Sanity
matched.overlap_description: Both axes track Carrasco's belief that Quixote can be managed or cured through staged schemes and combat, followed by the failure of that method; Set A emphasizes chastened acceptance, Set B emphasizes baffled denial.

matched.set_a_axis: From therapeutic correction to vengeful payback and back to custodial respect
matched.set_b_axis: From Benevolent Curer to Vindictive Avenger to Self-Justifying Physician
matched.overlap_description: Both axes track the moral framing of Carrasco's manipulation: initial benevolent cure, a vengeful phase after humiliation, and a final return to self-justifying care or custodianship.

unique_to_a.axis: From clever mastermind to humbled witness and elegist

unique_to_b.axis: From Unselfconscious Scheming to Displaced Partial Insight

matched.set_a_axis: From trusted confidant to concealed adversary to reconciled executor
matched.set_b_axis: From Amused Instrumental Curiosity to Antagonistic Rivalry to Patronizing Benevolence
matched.overlap_description: Partial overlap: Set B's Don Quixote axis includes confidant, concealment, rivalry, and reconciliation phases, though Set B labels the dimension as esteem/antagonism rather than trust/concealment.

matched.set_a_axis: From amused superiority to resentful rivalry to respectful memorial
matched.set_b_axis: From Amused Instrumental Curiosity to Antagonistic Rivalry to Patronizing Benevolence
matched.overlap_description: Strong overlap: both track Carrasco's emotional valuation of Quixote from amused superiority/curiosity through humiliating rivalry to warmer but still condescending remembrance.

matched.set_a_axis: From teasing superior to tactful co-concealer
matched.set_b_axis: From Instrumental Condescension to Affectionate Alliance
matched.overlap_description: Both track the Sancho relationship from teasing instrumental condescension toward warmer alliance, with residual superiority and guarded concealment.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Instrumental Self-Assertion to Communal Embeddedness
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Agency-dominant: Carrasco seeks centrality, mastery, and reputation through wit, flattery, disguise, and staged combat; relationships are largely instruments for managing Quixote, Sancho, and the village audience.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: More communally embedded but still patronizing: he embraces Quixote, collaborates with the curate on the pastoral scheme, allies warmly with Sancho, and serves as executor and epitaph-writer, though his sociability remains self-assured and condescending.

trajectory.phase: Playful social mastery and insider performance
trajectory.position_description: High agency and instrumental sociability: he flatters Quixote, teases Sancho, positions himself as a literary insider, and encourages the third sally while secretly conspiring to manage it.
key_moments: Returns from Salamanca with news of the printed history.
Flatters Quixote and probes Sancho about the book's omissions.
Advises the next sally and is trusted with the secret departure.
Dismisses the housekeeper's fears and supplies a helmet while secretly aligning with the curate and barber.

trajectory.position_description: Agency is asserted through disguise and combat, but the scheme collapses into humiliation; communion drops as he converts shame into private vengeance.
key_moments: Provokes Quixote as the Knight of the Mirrors.
Is violently unhorsed and exposed as Carrasco.
Is forced to confess Dulcinea's superiority and obey Quixote's terms.
Admits to Tom Cecial that he now wants to thrash Quixote out of vengeance.

trajectory.position_description: He remains strategic but shifts toward restrained procedure: skeptical verification, anonymity, formal challenge, and merciful terms rather than open personal domination.
key_moments: Questions the page and remains skeptical about Sancho's government.
Returns as the Knight of the White Moon and imposes a chivalric oath.
Defeats Quixote while sparing his body and Dulcinea's honor.
Leaves anonymously and reveals his identity only to Don Antonio.

trajectory.position_description: He moves toward communion: he embraces Quixote, enters the pastoral fiction, allies with Sancho, and serves as executor and elegist, though his care remains therapeutically condescending.
key_moments: Renews his plan after the Knight of the Mirrors defeat and collaborates with the duke.
Welcomes the returning Quixote with open arms and learns privately of the oath.
Applauds the pastoral plan and accepts the name 'Carrascon'.
Proposes pastoral names including 'Teresaina' for Sancho's wife.
Is appointed executor and composes Quixote's epitaph.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Both sets trace a real but incomplete movement from instrumental, competitive agency toward social participation, collaborative fiction-making, and village fellowship. Carrasco remains self-assured and patronizing throughout, so the increase in communion is genuine but mixed.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Engineered Control and Confident Cure to Chastened Acceptance and Baffled Denial
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Carrasco believes Don Quixote can be managed, defeated, and cured through clever schemes, flattery, disguise, and staged chivalric combat; deception is understood as medicine and his own method as lucid.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: His schemes are repeatedly refuted. He moves toward accepting that Quixote's cure, sanity, and death exceed his control, yet he also treats Quixote's final lucidity as a new symptom and never fully revises his belief in manipulation as cure.

trajectory.position_description: He treats Quixote as highly susceptible to admiration and literary fame and trusts social performance and engineered circumstances to direct or cure him.
key_moments: Uses flattery and literary talk to gain influence.
Advises the next sally and is trusted with secrecy.
Deceives the housekeeper while planning to encourage Quixote's departure.
Helps launch the third sally and conspires with the curate and barber.

trajectory.position_description: The Knight of the Mirrors plan backfires; his confidence in easy control is severely shaken, but he converts failure into vengeance rather than rethinking the method.
key_moments: Provokes Quixote into combat as the Knight of the Mirrors.
Is defeated and unmasked.
Is forced to confess Dulcinea's beauty and obey Quixote's terms.
Admits his plan failed and turns toward revenge.

trajectory.position_description: He learns that direct force and public unmasking fail, so he seeks control through anonymity, formal chivalric contract, restraint, and merciful terms.
key_moments: Calls Sancho's government delusion or enchantment.
Challenges Don Quixote as the Knight of the White Moon.
Defeats him without striking his body and imposes a year's retirement.
Leaves anonymously rather than seeking credit.
Tells Don Antonio his plan and asks for secrecy.

trajectory.position_description: He discovers that Quixote is already bound by his oath and later that Quixote's lucidity and death cannot be managed by Carrasco's pastoral scheme; he accepts a custodial role but denies the sanity as madness.
key_moments: Learns privately that Don Quixote has been defeated and is bound to stay home a year.
Applauds the pastoral plan as containment.
Hears Don Quixote declare that his reason has returned and urges him to 'be rational'.
Witnesses Quixote's rational confession and is appointed executor.
Writes an epitaph conceding that Quixote died sane without revising his own therapeutic method.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Both sets show repeated schemes failing. Set A emphasizes chastened acceptance of limits; Set B emphasizes baffled denial of Quixote's sanity. Merged, the arc is a disillusionment of therapeutic control: Carrasco's method is refuted in fact, but he only partially internalizes the lesson.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Benevolent Cure to Vengeful Payback to Self-Justifying Custodianship
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Carrasco frames his manipulations as benevolent correction: he presents himself as a conscientious friend and physician who must urge, persuade, and manage Don Quixote for Quixote's own good.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: After a vengeful phase and revised schemes, he returns to a benevolent self-justification as executor and elegist; he honors Quixote in death but never acknowledges the moral cost of his own manipulation.

trajectory.position_description: He presents his interference as prudence and care, builds trust through flattery and literary talk, and encourages the sally as a controlled cure.
key_moments: Cultivates Quixote and Sancho as a knowing friend.
Claims he would burden his conscience if he did not urge Quixote.
Encourages the third sally and presents himself as an oracle of Quixote's destiny.
Secretly arranges to follow and manage the sally.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat and exposure, his charitable aim collapses into resentment; he openly wants to thrash Quixote and rationalizes his own sanity against Quixote's madness.
key_moments: Is unhorsed and forced to confess Dulcinea's superiority.
Tells Tom Cecial he now wants revenge rather than a cure.
Stays behind meditating revenge while Quixote explains away the disguise as enchantment.

trajectory.position_description: He reframes his mission as a disciplined, benevolent correction: a formal challenge with merciful terms rather than public humiliation or personal vengeance.
key_moments: Challenges Don Quixote as the Knight of the White Moon.
Spares Quixote's life and Dulcinea's honor.
Prescribes retirement as a physician-like cure.
Frames his deception to Don Antonio as a cure for Quixote's madness and asks for secrecy.

trajectory.position_description: His corrective project gives way to companionship, respect, and executor duties, but he still justifies his fictions as care and tries to keep Quixote inside the therapeutic fiction.
key_moments: Embraces Don Quixote and promotes the pastoral scheme as a cure.
Urges Quixote to 'be rational' when Quixote announces sanity.
Endorses Sancho's denial of death.
Is appointed executor and composes an epitaph honoring Quixote.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Both sets see oscillation rather than clean moral conversion: benevolent cure, vengeful humiliation, disciplined correction, and finally custodial care. The recurrence of vengeance and self-justification makes the arc morally ambivalent rather than a clean ethical transformation.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Clever Mastermind to Humbled Witness with Limited Self-Awareness
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Carrasco sees himself as the clever social performer, indispensable insider, secret director, and architect of Don Quixote's destiny; he has little awareness that his staged deceptions mirror the fictions he criticizes in Quixote.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He accepts a final role as witness, executor, and elegist rather than victor over Quixote's madness; his epitaph concedes Quixote died sane, but he never applies that recognition to his own manipulations, vanity, or theatrical self-fabrication.

trajectory.position_description: He enjoys seeing himself as a skilled puppeteer managing Quixote's vanity, Sancho's touchiness, and the housekeeper's fears while believing himself the lucid physician of a madman.
key_moments: Uses flattery and literary praise to become Don Quixote's trusted confidant.
Manages Sancho through tactical flattery and retreat.
Promises the housekeeper miracles while secretly encouraging Quixote's departure.
Enjoys being the bearer of literary news and the knowing intermediary.

trajectory.position_description: His self-image is wounded by defeat, exposure, and forced submission; he becomes a beaten plotter who rationalizes failure and converts shame into resentment, missing the mirror held up by Tom Cecial's question about who is madder.
key_moments: Is defeated and unmasked as the Knight of the Mirrors.
Is forced to submit to Don Quixote's terms.
Admits his vengeful motive to Tom Cecial.
Accepts Quixote's enchanter explanation to save face.

trajectory.position_description: He partially restores his self-image through a successful, restrained victory, chooses anonymity over glory, and sees himself as a physician to Quixote's madness while never testing his own reality.
key_moments: Questions the page and calls Sancho's government a delusion.
Defeats Don Quixote as the Knight of the White Moon.
Refuses to linger or be identified.
Explains his plan to Don Antonio as a benevolent cure.
Laughs at the duke's mockeries without seeing himself as a comparable fabricator.

trajectory.position_description: His corrective role becomes irrelevant when Quixote's own oath and final lucidity take over; he accepts the role of executor and memorialist, with only a displaced flicker of insight in the epitaph.
key_moments: Welcomes Don Quixote home and proposes a shared pastoral life.
Urges Quixote to 'be rational' when Quixote announces his reason has returned.
Hears Quixote renounce chivalric madness.
Is appointed executor and composes an epitaph conceding that Quixote died sane without confessing his own role in the fictions.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Set A tracks the shift from mastermind self-image to humbled witness and elegist; Set B stresses that self-awareness remains minimal and displaced. Merged, Carrasco's role changes more than his insight: he memorializes Quixote without recognizing his own participation in the fictions that shaped him.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Trusted Confidant to Concealed Adversary to Reconciled Executor
relational_axes.pole_start: Mutual trust and intimacy: Don Quixote accepts Carrasco as an admiring friend, literary confidant, and secret adviser, while Carrasco gains access and leverage through flattery and concealed intentions.
relational_axes.pole_end: Reconciled trust and posthumous esteem: Don Quixote appoints Carrasco as executor, and Carrasco embraces the role of companion, mourner, and elegist, even though his earlier deceptions remain hidden.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco builds trust through theatrical flattery, literary discussion, advice, and secrecy. Don Quixote treats him as a trusted friend and confidant while Carrasco secretly plans to manage the sally.
key_moments: Kneels before Don Quixote and extravagantly praises him and the published history.
Reports the book's critics and draws out Don Quixote's defenses.
Advises the next sally and is asked to keep the departure secret.
Accepts the commission to compose acrostic verses for Dulcinea.
Dismisses the housekeeper's fears while conspiring with the curate and barber.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco becomes a hidden adversary through the Knight of the Mirrors disguise. After defeat, Don Quixote's belief in Carrasco's friendship ironically preserves the mask while Carrasco privately turns toward revenge.
key_moments: As the Knight of the Mirrors, provokes Don Quixote into combat.
Is defeated and exposed as Carrasco.
Is forced to confess Dulcinea's superiority and obey Quixote's terms.
Don Quixote explains the disguise as enchantment in Carrasco's favor, preserving the friendship fiction.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco refuses open identity and replaces personal friendship with concealed antagonism managed through chivalric form. He defeats Quixote mercifully but anonymously.
key_moments: Challenges Don Quixote as the Knight of the White Moon.
Defeats him while sparing his body and Dulcinea's honor.
Leaves without lingering or being identified.
Reveals his identity only to Don Antonio and asks secrecy.

trajectory.position_description: Concealed antagonism gives way to an embrace, shared pastoral play, and finally to Quixote's trust in Carrasco as executor. Carrasco memorializes him after death.
key_moments: Welcomes the returning Don Quixote with open arms.
Applauds and joins the pastoral plan as 'Carrascon'.
Witnesses Quixote's rational confession and is appointed executor.
Composes Don Quixote's epitaph.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Trust and concealment alternate: Carrasco first earns Quixote's confidence, then hides antagonism under disguise, and finally returns to a trusted companion and executor role after Quixote's oath and death. The reconciliation is real, but the earlier deceptions remain concealed.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Amused Superiority to Resentful Rivalry to Respectful but Patronizing Memorial
relational_axes.pole_start: Playful superiority: Carrasco sees Don Quixote as vain, thin-skinned, credulous, and easy to influence; genuine esteem is low and masked by flattery.
relational_axes.pole_end: Warm but patronizing posthumous esteem: Carrasco recognizes Quixote's dignified final lucidity only partially, memorializes him, and resolves antagonism into tribute while still treating him as a pitied patient.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco enjoys provoking Don Quixote's vanity and manipulating him. He regards Quixote as a vain dupe and himself as intellectually superior.
key_moments: Flatters Don Quixote while observing his susceptibility to admiration.
Draws out Don Quixote's defensive literary lecture.
Encourages the third sally while presenting himself as an oracle.

trajectory.position_description: Superiority turns into resentment after defeat. Don Quixote becomes a source of humiliation, and Carrasco's motive shifts from correction to vengeance.
key_moments: Is defeated and unmasked as the Knight of the Mirrors.
Is forced to submit to Don Quixote's terms.
Admits he wants to thrash Don Quixote out of pain and vengeance.
Meditates revenge after Tom Cecial leaves.

trajectory.position_description: Clinical contempt mixes with resentful rivalry. He wants Quixote humbled and his own theory vindicated.
key_moments: Remains vengeful after his defeat.
Calls Quixote's world enchantment or delusion.
Plans another disguised correction.

trajectory.position_description: Victory softens contempt into martial courtesy and pity. He treats Don Quixote as an opponent to be corrected rather than destroyed.
key_moments: Defeats Don Quixote as the Knight of the White Moon.
Spares Quixote's life and leaves Dulcinea's beauty unimpugned.
Prescribes a year of quiet and asks for secrecy.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco's esteem rises as he witnesses Quixote's oath-bound return and final sanity, but he cannot fully accept Quixote's own account of his lucidity. He ends as a mourner and elegist rather than a rival.
key_moments: Embraces Don Quixote and proposes a shared pastoral life.
Urges Quixote to 'be rational' when Quixote announces sanity.
Hears Quixote renounce chivalric madness.
Is appointed executor and composes an epitaph honoring Quixote.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Carrasco moves from amused contempt for Don Quixote's vanity, through humiliating rivalry, to restrained correction and finally respectful memorialization. The net direction is positive, though his final esteem remains condescending and he never fully accepts Quixote's sanity.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Instrumental Condescension to Affectionate and Guarded Alliance
relational_axes.pole_start: Carrasco treats Sancho as a comic simpleton and useful conduit: amusing, gullible, and socially inferior, while Sancho remains friendly but guarded about personal matters.
relational_axes.pole_end: Warmly condescending alliance: Carrasco teases Sancho affectionately, folds him into the pastoral joke, and shares the deathbed grief, though he still regards him as comic and limited; a residue of guarded mutual concealment remains.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco establishes a mild intellectual hierarchy over Sancho, teasing him and testing his credibility, then retreats into flattery when Sancho becomes defensive.
key_moments: Reports the book's omissions and inserted novel, drawing out Sancho's evasive excuses.
Probes Sancho about the stolen ass and missing hundred crowns.
Backs off, praises Sancho's answer, and promises to have the historian include it.
Corrects his grammar with amusement.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is a comic instrument and lever, kept busy by a hired proxy while the knights fight.
key_moments: Uses Tom Cecial to flatter and distract Sancho.
Judges Sancho 'one of the greatest simpletons of modern times'.
Shows little concern for Sancho's role in the failed plot.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho doubts the enchantment story around the Knight of the Mirrors but does not expose Carrasco; both remain undeclared, preserving a guarded, ambivalent trust.
key_moments: Sancho doubts the enchantment explanation but withholds his own deception.
Carrasco's secret identity remains protected by mutual concealment.

trajectory.position_description: Open contempt: he calls Sancho's government a delusion or enchantment and vows to drive it out of his head.
key_moments: Doubts the reality of Sancho's island government.
Wants to physically verify the page as flesh and blood.
Is reported as intending to correct Sancho forcibly.

trajectory.position_description: Affectionate amusement becomes practical alliance. He includes Sancho in the shared fiction, christens Teresa 'Teresaina,' and shares the deathbed grief, though he still treats Sancho as comic and limited.
key_moments: Joins the shepherd fraternity and proposes pastoral names, including one for Sancho's wife.
Treats Sancho as part of the communal game.
Says 'good Sancho Panza's view of these cases is quite right.'
Uses Sancho as reinforcement against Quixote's sanity and participates in the collective grief.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The Sancho relationship warms from instrumental teasing and guarded concealment to affectionate alliance. The change is modest: Carrasco never treats Sancho as an equal, and his esteem rises only into warmer condescension.

matched.set_a_axis: From Dominant Hospitality to Entrenched Manipulative Control
matched.set_b_axis: From bored dominative control to consolidated instrumental dominance
matched.overlap_description: Both axes use the Agency vs Communion dimension and describe the same trajectory: aristocratic hospitality is a performative mask for control, which escalates from playful staging through elaborate hoaxes to abduction and dismissal. Both conclude that the communion pole never becomes genuine and that agency merely becomes more systematized.

matched.set_a_axis: From Oblivious Amusement to Momentary Remorse then Rationalized Persistence
matched.set_b_axis: From unexamined cruelty to still-unexamined cruelty
matched.overlap_description: Both track moral accountability/self-awareness and agree that the pair treats suffering as comic material, that the only check is the brief grief after the ch.99 cat prank, and that this regret is practical rather than ethical. Both conclude there is no moral learning; B additionally locates the moral judgment in the narrator rather than the characters.

unique_to_a.axis: From Benevolent Hosts to Entitled Gamemasters (Self-Image as Host)

matched.set_a_axis: From Celebrated Guest to Staged Plaything (Don Quixote)
matched.set_b_axis: From mock-revered guest to disposable captive spectacle (Don Quixote)
matched.overlap_description: Both describe ceremonial, mock-reverent reception of Quixote as a famous knight-performer that degrades into instrumentalization. B adds the final stage absent from A: the night abduction at lance-point, the catafalque pageant, and the coldly easy dismissal, which sharpen the endpoint from 'plaything' to 'disposable captive'.

matched.set_a_axis: From Amusing Companion to Exploited Comic Dependent (Sancho Panza)
matched.set_b_axis: From patronized clown to prized comic specimen (Sancho Panza)
matched.overlap_description: Both describe real fondness and amusement that function as leverage: the island promise, the Barataria hoax, Clavileño, and the culminating physical torment in the resurrection pageant. They diverge in emphasis: A stresses deepening exploitation, B stresses a slight rise in esteem ('marvel at his simplicity and sharpness') while noting trust and moral respect never rise and debts go unpaid. Merged, the axis is warm amusement plus persistent instrumentalization.

unique_to_a.axis: From Flattered Servant to Punished Intruder (Doña Rodriguez)

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Dominant Hospitality to Consolidated Instrumental Dominance
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Aristocratic self-assertion masked as hospitality: they welcome Don Quixote and Sancho with ceremony while privately treating them as material for amusement; any communion is staged, patronizing warmth.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Agentic control is fully consolidated and systematized: control exercised through proxies, abduction, punishment, and theatrical cruelty, with communion entirely simulated and instrumental.

trajectory.position_description: Absent throughout the First Part and early Second Part; framed only as aristocratic patrons whose introduction will serve spectacle.
key_moments: No appearance before ch.83; their acquaintance with the heroes is owed to the narrative's convenience.

trajectory.position_description: Firmly on the agency pole: they resolve to fall in with Quixote's humor, stage a reverent reception, and treat guests as raw material; warmth is performative.
key_moments: They decide to humor Don Quixote's madness as entertainment.
Mock-reverent reception of Quixote as 'Knight of the Lions'; seating him at the head of the table.
The Duchess enjoys Sancho's drollery, invites him to ride beside her, and promises the island.
The Duke laughs off the ecclesiastic's moral rebuke and the pair conspire to devise new pranks.

trajectory.position_description: Agency intensifies into elaborate stage-management and proxy control; communion with both guests is entirely instrumental.
key_moments: Staged supernatural hunt and Merlin's demand for Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Pressure on Sancho to accept the 3,300 lashes; the Clavileño flight hoax.
Barataria puppet government with a majordomo instructed to deceive.
Forged warning of assassins and poison to keep the guests dependent.

trajectory.position_description: Control remains the governing mode but must be repaired through punishment, substitution, and containment when servants or guests act off-script; a brief check after the cat prank does not alter the pattern.
key_moments: The cat prank injures Don Quixote and they are briefly grieved.
The Duchess flogs Doña Rodriguez and torments Quixote out of wounded vanity.
The Duke substitutes the counterfeit knight Tosilos, then has him flogged.
Mock theft quarrel over garters at the departure.

trajectory.position_description: Agency peaks in silent capture and staged resurrection; the pair preside over torment and then dismiss Quixote with easy courtesy. Communion is absent.
key_moments: Quixote and Sancho abducted at lance-point and held as captive audience.
Catafalque pageant with Altisidora's staged resurrection and Sancho's ritual humiliation.
The Duke deliberately orchestrates the final hoax for his own amusement; Quixote released 'very readily.'

trajectory.position_description: Offstage and unchanged; their props and unpaid promises linger while their psychology remains fixed on the agency pole.
key_moments: Altisidora's promised smocks remain unpaid.
The flame-painted robe and mitre become village comedy.
Quixote dies without them; Cide Hamete implies the contrivers are as foolish as the victims.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Across every appearance from ch.83 onward, the Duke and Duchess seek mastery rather than mutuality. Hospitality is stagecraft, gifts are levers, and the culmination is abduction and dismissal. The communion pole never becomes genuine at any point; agency only becomes more systematized and better resourced, making this an entrenching (negative) rather than transformative arc.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Unexamined Cruelty to Still-Unexamined Cruelty (Brief Regret Without Reflection)
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: No awareness that making madness and credulity into entertainment is cruel; exploitation is framed as hospitality, wit, and aristocratic sport.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Still no moral self-knowledge. Brief regret after the cat prank and repeated exposure of consequences produce no ethical reflection; the narrator, not the characters, delivers judgment.

trajectory.position_description: Self-aware only as impresarios, never as exploiters; laughter at humiliation is treated as proof of clever hosting, and external moral challenge is dismissed.
key_moments: The ecclesiastic rebukes the Duke; the rebuke is laughed off.
Clavileño and Distressed Duenna hoaxes staged without self-critique.
Delight in Sancho's letter and credulity; resolve to continue because 'no reality amuses them more.'

trajectory.position_description: The bell-and-cat prank injures Quixote, producing alarm and grief, but no examination of the ethics of the game.
key_moments: Quixote wounded and bedridden by the night-time cat prank.
The Duke and Duchess are 'greatly grieved' that the joke fell heavily on him, then quickly resume plotting.

trajectory.position_description: They intensify pressure and humiliation; when the Barataria joke overshoots, servants feel the pity the masters lack.
key_moments: Forged assassin-and-poison warning.
Sancho faints under mock justice; the jokers are 'sorry they had pushed it so far' but the principals do not reflect.
The Duchess punishes Doña Rodriguez and torments Quixote out of wounded vanity.

trajectory.position_description: Tosilos's conscience is an inconvenience, Doña Rodriguez's grievance is comic material, and violence is administered to preserve the script.
key_moments: Tosilos exposed as counterfeit, flogged, and sent on an errand.
The Duke turns a deaf ear to Doña Rodriguez's grievance during the Tosilos disruption.
Altisidora's outburst managed as jest.

trajectory.position_description: They stage abduction and mock resurrection; the narrator judges the contrivers as mad as the victims, while they remain unaware of any moral problem.
key_moments: Silent night abduction at lance-point.
Sancho pinched, pricked, and smacked in the catafalque pageant.
Cide Hamete says the Duke and Duchess are 'not two fingers' breadth' from folly.

trajectory.position_description: Offstage to the end; no self-scrutiny occurs and their unpaid debts and discarded props go unacknowledged.
key_moments: Altisidora's smocks left unpaid.
The buckram robe and mitre kept as village relics.
No appearance at Quixote's death.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The pair never moves from ethical blindness to insight. The single clear opportunity is ch.99, but the regret is practical rather than moral, and it does not change behavior. Later chapters repeatedly display consequences—Sancho's fainting, Tosilos's beating, Doña Rodriguez's punishment—without altering the ducal self-image. Moral reasoning is flat: amusement repeatedly overrides accountability, and any judgment comes from the narrator rather than the characters.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Benevolent Hosts to Entitled Gamemasters
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: They see themselves as sophisticated, generous, playful hosts indulging a harmless fantasy, and as patrons rewarding a deserving squire.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: They see themselves as master illusionists entitled to stage guests' lives for amusement; benevolence survives only as a veneer and as self-justification.

trajectory.position_description: They understand themselves as gracious hosts and playful patrons; their self-story is flattering and internally coherent.
key_moments: They welcome Don Quixote with chivalric ceremony and seat him at the head of the table.
The Duke grants Sancho a government in front of the ecclesiastic.
The Duke protects Don Quixote from discovering the beard-washing prank.

trajectory.position_description: Self-image hardens around clever stage-management and control of spectacle.
key_moments: They plot new knight-errantry jokes after Sancho's confession.
Staging of fake disenchantment, Merlin, the Distressed Duenna, and Clavileño.
They resolve to prolong the deception through Sancho's governorship.

trajectory.position_description: After a brief check, they reassert themselves as entitled directors of guest lives; benevolence persists only as a rhetorical cover for humiliation.
key_moments: The Duchess avenges her wounded vanity through humiliation.
The Duke converts Tosilos's disruption into another controlled game.
They stage the final resurrection spectacle and Sancho's humiliation, then grant him the robe and mitre as a mock memento.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Their self-perception does not transform; it hardens. Manipulation is continuously justified through a self-image of generous, ingenious hospitality, and the language of gift and patronage survives to the end as the covering for spectacle. This axis is closely related to the Agency vs Communion axis—it is the internal narrative that licenses the agentic behavior—and should be treated as a supporting facet rather than an independent psychological change.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Mock-Revered Guest-Performer to Disposable Captive Spectacle
relational_axes.pole_start: Condescending fascination masked as profound respect: Quixote is a prized guest-performer and famous knight whose illusion is ceremonially protected, though esteem is genuinely low and intimacy theatrical.
relational_axes.pole_end: Quixote is a discarded anecdote and captive prop: abducted at lance-point, tormented as a captive audience, then released with easy courtesy; esteem, trust, and intimacy are all low.

trajectory.position_description: Exaggerated chivalric courtesy combined with private condescension; they honor his knightly identity and preserve his dignity because the illusion is useful.
key_moments: They await Don Quixote with delight and decide to humor his delusions.
Embrace and title 'Sir Knight of the Lions'; seating him at the head of the table.
The Duke suppresses laughter and protects the illusion during the beard-washing prank.

trajectory.position_description: They flatter and stage him in increasingly elaborate hoaxes; his credulity is useful and amusing rather than respected.
key_moments: Staged disenchantment of Dulcinea and Merlin's demand.
The Distressed Duenna and Clavileño spectacles.
They flatter him as a famous knight whose aid is sought; Altisidora's serenade.

trajectory.position_description: The cat prank wounds him and they briefly worry over a damaged plaything, then ignore his hints of departure and absorb him into new games.
key_moments: Bell-and-cat injury leaves Quixote bedridden; they are briefly grieved.
Quixote's letter hints he may leave; new diversions displace him.
The Duchess torments him after Doña Rodriguez's indiscretion.

trajectory.position_description: He is pointed at staged combat and mocked at departure; courtesy remains performative and control remains theirs.
key_moments: Tosilos combat staged for Quixote's benefit.
Mock quarrel over garters and mock accusation at his leaving.
Polite but shallow farewell.

trajectory.position_description: They reverse earlier indifference, capture him at night, hold him as captive audience, and then release him 'very readily'; intimacy falls to its lowest point.
key_moments: Silent abduction at lance-point.
Catafalque pageant in which he is forced to witness Sancho's torment.
Dismissal with easy courtesy; the Duke deliberately orchestrates the final hoax.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The relationship moves from apparent honor to open instrumentalization. Esteem never becomes genuine, and intimacy declines from theatrical closeness to cold disposal. Outward courtesy persists throughout as a shell, but the endpoint—night abduction, captive audience, casual release—confirms that Quixote is a consumable spectacle rather than a guest.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Patronized Comic Dependent to Tormented, Marveled-At Specimen
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho is a beloved buffoon: the Duchess delights in his drollery, calls him 'discreet,' invites him into intimacy, and promises him an island, while trust and esteem remain low.
relational_axes.pole_end: Sancho is still instrumentalized and physically tormented for spectacle, though the pair now marvel at his blend of simplicity and sharpness; esteem rises to medium while trust, equality, and paid debts do not.

trajectory.position_description: Positive intimacy and condescending esteem; Sancho is a valued but comic guest whose credulity is already being harvested.
key_moments: The Duchess enjoys Sancho's drollery, calls him 'very discreet,' and invites him to ride beside her.
The Duchess questions him about Dulcinea and professes belief to soothe Don Quixote.
She privately receives Sancho's confession and reaffirms the promised island.

trajectory.position_description: Affection mixes with exploitation as Sancho becomes the central comic engine of the hoaxes; his fears and proverbs are harvested for laughter.
key_moments: They exploit his fear during the staged disenchantment and pressure him toward the 3,300 lashes.
The Duke and Duchess steer him onto Clavileño.
They despatch him to the fake island of Barataria with a majordomo instructed to deceive him.
They are greatly amused by reports of his misadventures.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho governs more wisely than scripted and leaves Barataria with dignity; the intended submission scene is denied, though their esteem does not yet openly rise.
key_moments: Sancho out-talks the jesters and refuses to account to anyone but the Duke.
He faints under mock justice; the jokers, not the principals, feel the pity.

trajectory.position_description: They welcome him back with embraces and vague promises of another post, still treating him as a beloved clown and comic witness.
key_moments: Ropes haul Sancho and Dapple from the pit.
Promise of a less onerous post; the majordomo secretly gives him money.

trajectory.position_description: Negative exploitation intensifies as mock benevolence accompanies ritual humiliation; simultaneously their curiosity about him deepens into grudging admiration, though nothing is repaid.
key_moments: Sancho receives smacks, pinches, and pinpricks to revive Altisidora.
The Duchess grants him the flame robe and mitre as a mock memento.
The Duke and Duchess marvel at his 'simplicity' and 'sharpness.'
Altisidora's promised smocks remain unpaid.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Their fondness for Sancho is real but instrumental, and it grows warmer as his comic value grows. The two analyses diverge only in emphasis: the event graph stresses deepening exploitation, the psychological summary stresses a slight rise in esteem. Both are true—amusement and admiration increase while trust, moral respect, and reciprocity never do—and the relationship culminates in physical torment staged as court entertainment, with debts left unpaid. The shift is from simple patronized clown to prized and wondered-at specimen, not toward equality.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Flattered Servant to Punished Intruder
relational_axes.pole_start: The Duchess flatters Doña Rodriguez and manages her grievance as manageable social theater, treating her with condescending favor.
relational_axes.pole_end: The Duchess punishes her for indiscretion and the Duke shows indifference to her grievance, subordinating her entirely to the joke.

trajectory.position_description: Condescending favor; the Duchess manages the duenna dispute through flattery and redirection toward Sancho's anti-duenna prejudice.
key_moments: The Duchess flatters Doña Rodriguez and redirects the dispute toward Sancho's prejudice against duennas.

trajectory.position_description: Wounded vanity turns favor into open hostility and physical punishment.
key_moments: The Duchess overhears Doña Rodriguez's indiscretion and is enraged.
She bursts into Don Quixote's room, torments him, and flogs the duenna.

trajectory.position_description: Astonishment and patronizing indulgence replace simple contempt, but respect remains absent.
key_moments: The Duke and Duchess are astonished by Doña Rodriguez's bold plea.
The Duchess orders the women treated as lady adventurers rather than servants.

trajectory.position_description: The Duke ignores her grievance to sustain the joke, confirming punitive disregard.
key_moments: The Duke turns a deaf ear to Doña Rodriguez's grievance and humiliation during the Tosilos disruption.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The relationship moves from condescending favor to punitive control. Doña Rodriguez is valued only insofar as she serves the household spectacle; when her grievance threatens the script she is beaten, then ignored. This axis was present only in the event-graph analysis and remains a valid but secondary relationship, consistent with the pair's treatment of all subordinates as stage property.
